text:
WASHINGTON — As many as 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children are at risk of losing their federally funded legal representation due to the Trump administration withholding appropriated funds, immigration attorneys warned Tuesday.

For more than six months, the Health and Human Services Department’s Office of Refugee Resettlement has not released $65 million Congress appropriated for legal representation of unaccompanied children in immigration cases. That means children may have to press their immigration claims on their own, vastly raising the probability they will be deported, the attorneys said.

“Children are now facing the real possibility of representing themselves alone against experienced government attorneys,” Ana Devereaux, an attorney at the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center, said during a virtual press conference.

Shaina Aber, the executive director for Acacia Center for Justice, a national group that partners with at least 100 legal organizations to provide services to children, said the lack of funding is already being felt. Several of the group’s partners have declined to continue the partnerships because they have not been reimbursed, she said.

Aber said the funds were withheld because attorneys refused to hand over to the administration sensitive case data from the unaccompanied children, such as medical records and the types of legal relief the minors are seeking.

“These children should not, and should never be, leveraged in a political game,” she said.

HHS did not respond to States Newsroom's request for comment.

‘Children are children’

Without a lawyer, fewer than 10% of immigrant children win the right to remain in the United States while their case goes through immigration court, said Elizabeth Young, a former immigration judge.

Some children going through the courts are too young to speak, she said during the press conference.

“A legal system that values fairness cannot expect children to carry that burden alone,” Young said.

Devereaux said the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center is operating on reserves and has continued to provide legal services for about 1,100 children.

“Children are children, regardless of their nationality,” Devereaux said.

Stripping away the legal services for children, Aber said, is “yet another system of mass deportations.”

Additionally, the Trump administration does not plan to renew its contract with Acacia, which ends July 31, Aber said.

Instead, the administration is eyeing a small Texas state commission that aids low-income people with criminal defense to provide legal services for immigrant children. The commission does not have experience handling immigration cases or unaccompanied minors, Aber said.

Lawmakers push to release funds

Democratic members of Congress have also called on the Trump administration to release the funds, which Congress approved.

Last month, more than 70 lawmakers demanded that ORR reimburse the legal groups.

“Ultimately, we are concerned that these payment delays may be an attempt to circumvent requirements that ORR continue funding legal services for unaccompanied children,” they wrote. “The federal government must meet its obligations under the law.”

Congress created the Unaccompanied Children Program, which, among other things, provides funding for legal representation of migrant children. Free legal representation is not generally provided for immigrants but there is a carveout for unaccompanied children.

There are about 100 organizations across the U.S. that provide those legal services.

The move from the Trump administration to withhold funds has sparked several lawsuits. Last year, a preliminary injunction was put in place that ordered the federal government to continue funding legal services for unaccompanied children.

But advocates have not received any funds since December and were back in court this month.

Last week, federal Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the U.S. District Court for the District of Northern California probed whether the Trump administration should be held in contempt over the withholding of funds after 11 groups claimed they have still not received any reimbursements, according to El Paso Matters.

Those groups are the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, Community Legal Services in East Palo Alto, Estrella del Paso, Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project, Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, Immigrant Defenders Law Center, National Immigrant Justice Center, Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network, Social Justice Collaborative and the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project.

In the five-page order, he wrote, “The consequences faced by plaintiffs are potentially severe.” The order will stay in place while he considers whether to issue a longer-term injunction, with a decision expected by August 5.

text:
By Sarah Nelson

Star Tribune

MINNEAPOLIS — A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit by the Justice Department targeting Minnesota’s laws prohibiting law enforcement from assisting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, saying state and local laws do not intrude on federal authority.

In a 56-page order, Chief U.S. District Judge Eric Tostrud rejected the Justice Department’s claims that Minnesota’s laws unfairly target federal immigration agents and inhibit them from carrying out immigration work.

| REGISTER: Building public confidence in an era of public safety innovation

“They do not command the federal government or its contractors to act. They do not forbid the federal government or its contractors from acting. They do not control how the federal government or its contractors undertake their work. Rather, they regulate how state and local officials perform their duties,” wrote Tostrud, a President Donald Trump appointee.

The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to the Minnesota Star Tribune’s request for comment about the order.

Filed in September, the lawsuit preceded Operation Metro Surge — the immigration crackdown in Minnesota that sent roughly 4,000 agents to the state. The administration asked the court to declare Minnesota’s policies unconstitutional and prohibit the state from enforcing them. In addition to suing the state, the Trump administration also sued Minneapolis, St. Paul and Hennepin County over ordinances that limited assistance with immigration enforcement.

The targeted policies included a prohibition on sharing driver’s license information with federal immigration agents and ordinances limiting what local police can share with federal immigration officers. Lawyers for the state and cities argued they should not be responsible for enforcing civil immigration law.

“Minnesota is not impeding immigration law, it is just not assisting,” wrote attorneys for the state in response to the lawsuit.

In his order, Tostrud said forcing Minnesota or cities to assist with civil federal immigration policies would violate the anticommandeering doctrine under the 10th Amendment, which prevents the federal government from compelling states to carry out its orders. He determined that forcing states to assist in federal immigration matters may cause the state budgetary concerns by shifting resources toward enforcing federal law.

He also rejected the federal government’s claims that Minnesota’s immigration laws single out the federal government, saying Minnesota laws also extend to private companies and state governments.

In a statement, Attorney General Keith Ellison praised the ruling and said Tostrud’s order “reaffirmed longstanding principle that the federal government cannot force Minnesota or any state to participate in its misguided immigration-enforcement efforts or commandeer state resources for it.”

“The Trump Administration , however, has no regard for this constitutional principle, so it nonetheless filed this lawsuit as part of its ongoing war against the people of Minnesota and its efforts to intimidate us into submission,” Ellison’s statement said. “They keep learning over and over that the people of Minnesota won’t be intimidated. Nor will I.”

The Trump administration has continued to make immigration a cornerstone of the president’s second term and target jurisdictions that have so-called “sanctuary” policies.

Last week, Maryland was among the latest to face a a Justice Department lawsuit over its laws. Some federal courts across the U.S. have dismissed similar lawsuits brought by the Justice Department , including in Los Angeles, Illinois, New Jersey and New York.

The suit against Minnesota came after Trump issued an executive order to identify jurisdictions that defy federal immigration law. Minnesota was later listed among a dozen states by the Justice Department for being a “sanctuary jurisdiction.”

title: Trump's Debanking Plan Will Boost Self-Deportations | FAIRUS.org
description:
By directing regulators to treat lack of legal work authorization as a serious credit risk, the new debanking policy has the potential to be a self-deportation engine.
This, in tandem with physical barriers, E-Verify expansion, and workplace enforcement, represents the smartest remedies for illegal mass migration in generations.
Mass illegal migration cannot be solved by border enforcement alone.
The United States has both the right and the responsibility to decide who may participate fully in its economy.
The Trump administration’s debanking guidance is a practical innovation that strengthens deterrence, encourages self-deportation, protects American workers and taxpayers, and reinforces the rule of law.
text:
When asked after his capture in 1952 why he robbed banks, the notorious Willie Sutton is alleged to have said “that’s where the money is.” Despite voluminous research and analysis of America’s problems with illegal migration, Sutton’s famous quote is the best explanation why foreign nationals still try to break into the United States.

The magnet that lures noncitizens to break our immigration laws isn’t just jobs, but also access to direct deposit, credit cards, and a bank account. The Trump administration’s May 2026 executive order drew a roadmap to restrict that system, and now it is being implemented. That’s good news for those weary of an immigration system that looks the other way at rampant lawlessness while ignoring policies that result in greater self-deportation.

By directing regulators to treat lack of legal work authorization as a serious credit risk, the new debanking policy has the potential to be a self-deportation engine. It is low-cost and ruthlessly effective at drying up the shadow economy that attracts a seemingly infinite supply of border crossers.

The rush of foreign national to cross our borders illegally is not primarily a humanitarian crisis at the border, but an economic phenomenon driven by jobs, wages, housing, and financial services inside the United States. Migrants come because employers can hire them, pay them, and integrate them into the economy. Access to bank accounts, direct deposit, credit cards, auto loans, and mortgages allow people here illegally to live better than they did in their homelands and to send remittances home. Remove or sharply restrict that access, and the decision to come here illegally is not the no-brainer it has been until now.

The policy works through straightforward risk management already embedded in existing law. Under guidance from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and banking regulators, lenders must assess a borrower’s ability to repay. When repayment depends on employment that can legally end at any moment through deportation or employer compliance with immigration law, that risk rises.

Banks have every incentive to avoid losses. The administration has simply clarified that immigration status and work authorization are relevant data points in that analysis. This is not a blanket prohibition. It is targeted scrutiny that ties private-sector incentives with national interest.

This strategy is practical because it leverages institutions that already exist and operate at scale. Banks already flag suspicious activity for anti-money laundering purposes. Adding immigration-related risk factors requires no new federal bureaucracy or army of agents.

Physical removals are also expensive and require significant human resources. Self-deportation through economic pressure is cheaper and faster.

For those who claim to generally support deportations but get the ick from watching how ICE does it, the debanking plan achieves the same goals without the sometimes violent altercations. Physical removals are also expensive and require significant human resources. Self-deportation through economic pressure is cheaper and faster. More than 2 million illegal aliens have self-deported in the second Trump administration. Imagine how many more will opt out when privileges like banking, credit, and stable payroll become unreliable.

The strategy also deters future illegal entries. Potential migrants must weigh the border crossing risks, employment prospects, and long-term viability. If the message is clear that the United States will no longer provide easy financial access in an increasingly cashless society for those here illegally, fewer will make the journey. This, in tandem with physical barriers, E-Verify expansion, and workplace enforcement, represents the smartest remedies for illegal mass migration in generations.

Critics may claim this directive burdens families or disrupts communities. The reality is that being in America illegally itself creates those burdens via overcrowded schools, hospitals, and housing markets, as well as wage competition for lower-skilled American workers. The policy does not target legal immigrants or citizens. It focuses solely on individuals who entered or remained in violation of U.S. law. The result will be safer, less crowded and more prosperous communities for those with the legal right to be here.

Mass illegal migration cannot be solved by border enforcement alone. Pull factors in the interior of the country must be addressed. Jobs are the primary magnet, and access to banking and credit sustains that magnet. Cutting off or complicating that access is a direct response that requires neither new statutes nor unlimited enforcement budgets. It turns the financial sector’s natural caution into an ally of immigration enforcement.

The United States has both the right and the responsibility to decide who may participate fully in its economy. The Trump administration’s debanking guidance is a practical innovation that strengthens deterrence, encourages self-deportation, protects American workers and taxpayers, and reinforces the rule of law. Other tools remain necessary, but this one deserves recognition as an efficient force multiplier in the effort to end the era of unchecked illegal mass migration.

text:
CLIFTON PARK — Nothing is taking Johan Sandoval’s eyes off the ball — not 13 days in a federal detention center, an ankle monitor, nor a potentially lengthy legal process to correct an error in paperwork that upended his immigration status.

“They will not kill my dream,” the standout student-athlete from Savannah State University told the Times Union following his recent release from an immigration detention center near Buffalo. “My professional dream is to play baseball. Even if I don’t play in America, I will find a way. It’s been my dream for a long time.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Sandoval, a 22-year-old from the Dominican Republic, whom his attorney said has no criminal record, was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on July 3 at an apartment he was staying at with his fiancée and her mother in Clifton Park. ICE officials said he was detained after agents found that a form he used to obtain a student visa expired in April 2025. He was released from federal custody on Wednesday on a $20,000 bond and ordered to wear an ankle monitor so ICE could track his movements.

An attorney for Sandoval has argued that the lapse was not his client’s fault and that the paperwork error likely happened when school officials did not update his transfer status after he left Bryant & Stratton College in 2024. He had departed for school at Savannah State in Georgia.

Sandoval said he will do what it takes to satisfy the orders from the immigration judge presiding over his case so that he can return to school and the sport he has loved since age 3. But he knows it’s not going to be easy.

On Friday, he still expressed shock over the whole ordeal: being blocked by federal agents while exiting the Clifton Park apartment complex, the act of being handcuffed and arrested, then locked up for nearly two weeks in the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in Batavia.

“When I first got arrested, I thought, ‘Why am I here?’” he said. “I do nothing wrong. I’m a good student. I’m a good athlete. I do community service. It was really bad.”

His first stop after his arrest was at the ICE field office in Malta, where he was processed. Later that day, he was transferred to Batavia. He said he was placed in a large room with several other detainees, where he lay on the floor for two days without sleeping because there were no available beds in the unit.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“It was a nightmare,” he recalled. “I kept trying to realize what was going on and ask God to guide me. I know how strong He is and I just kept praying for my family because I knew this was hard on my mom and dad.”

He went two days without contact with the outside world, until he was given a PIN code for the phone and a commissary at the site. He was placed in a unit he said was designated for people without criminal records.

“I had a hard battle in my mind,” Sandoval said. “The first week, I started losing hope. (Being detained was) killing my hopes. I felt no one here is going to help you. I didn’t know what time it was, what day it was. But God is great. He was always with me.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Once in his unit, things somewhat improved. He met people from the Caribbean and other Latin American countries. “We have a lot in common,” he noted.

He said they gathered for Bible studies and played baseball in a recreation area. They used their sandals for bases, their hands as bats, and a small ball the detention center provided to detainees. He said he also spent time doing pull-ups and sprinting short distances in the unit.

Since childhood, Sandoval prided himself on doing the right thing by his parents — focusing on school while pursuing his passion for baseball. Going to college in America seemed like the perfect plan.

He transferred to Savannah State University after obtaining an associate degree at Bryant & Stratton. As a Tiger, he became one of the college’s top players, starting every game as a second baseman with a strong batting average. At the end of the spring season, he was named to the ABCA/Rawlings NCAA Division II All-South Region Second Team.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

He met his fiancée, Adriana Wade, while he was in school in Albany. He was spending the summer with Wade and her mother, Lynn Tiberio, when ICE arrested him at their apartment complex.

When the Times Union reached out to ICE earlier this month to ask about Sandoval’s arrest, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said he tried to evade agents, but the agency did not immediately respond to a follow-up request asking for evidence of that. Tiberio disputes that Sandoval tried to run away. She said during the incident, she told Sandoval to wait on the balcony while she spoke with officers. When he came back inside, she said, he fully cooperated with offering his paperwork and when they subsequently took him into custody.

Sandoval’s attorney, John Jeha, said he is unsure why ICE is saying his client tried to flee. He also said it appeared that the immigration form the school fills out to certify the student’s eligibility for enrollment was changed after Sandoval graduated from Bryant & Stratton. It was coded in a database to “terminate” instead of “transfer.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

On Monday, another attorney for Sandoval, L.J. D’Arrigo, said Sandoval’s transfer was therefore never initiated with Savannah State.

The system also never alerted Sandoval to the change.

Savannah State University officials have not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, someone at the university told NewsChannel 13 that the school was not responsible for the error. Bryant & Stratton College officials also have not responded to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, Jeha said Sandoval is being treated like a criminal by the Department of Homeland Security.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“The $20,000 bond and ankle monitor is excessive and unnecessary,” said Jeha, who is based in Syracuse. “He is a superstar on the team. He has a public persona. He’s not hiding. What they are doing is completely wrong.”

He said Sandoval remains fearful he could be re-arrested.

“I fear (agents) will come back and do something against me,” he said. “I can’t leave the house alone.”

Jeha plans to accompany him to check in with immigration officials in Malta this week. Jeha is also fairly confident that Sandoval will be able to return to Savannah in the fall, as that was part of his bond agreement. But he said it is unlikely Sandoval will be able to work out or play baseball if he has to continue wearing an ankle monitor.

Expecting that issues with his immigration status will be costly, his family has been seeking donations through a GoFundMe campaign.

Though the situation has been trying, Sandoval said, “Everything happens for a reason.” He said he harbors no ill will toward ICE or the guards at the detention center and that he prays for them.

“God is always with me and gives me strength,” he said. “Even though bad things happen, I know He is still there for me. I had brothers that didn’t speak to each other. We are now all talking to each other, and I am grateful for that.”

text:
Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney said Monday that the Trump administration will lose a legal battle with The New York Times over journalists that reported on President Trump’s new Air Force One plane.

“My guess is, the administration will lose this. I’m not sure what the basis is for a lawsuit. Was there a national security leak? I have no idea. Again, I can’t leak anything because I don’t know anything, now, about it,” Mulvaney told NewsNation’s Connell McShane on “NewsNation Live.”

“I just know how it works generally, and I would be asking the exact same questions The New York Times was asking. So look, look when Trump, you know, when he gets upset, he lashes out, and I understand that,” added Mulvaney, who is a contributor to NewsNation.

Earlier this month, the Trump administration hit four Times journalists with subpoenas in the wake of the newspaper publishing a story outlining risks involving the security of the new Air Force One plane gifted to the president by Qatar. The plane just recently entered service for the administration.

The Times reported that the jet did not have some of the advanced security measures of the older aircraft used for the president’s transportation.

Julian E. Barnes, Eric Lipton, Tyler Pager and Eric Schmitt were among the reporters hit with the subpoenas. The reporters earlier that week wrote that a security precaution resulted in the president leaving a NATO summit in Turkey on the old Air Force One.

The Times journalists were called to testify before a federal grand jury in New York City “in regard to an alleged violation of federal criminal law.”

text:
The Mexican man who officials say was killed by a truck last week in St. Augustine, Florida, while running from immigration officers was identified by a farmworkers’ advocacy group as a father of two on vacation with a valid tourist visa.

Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran, 28, was visiting from his hometown of San Luis de La Paz, a small city in the central state of Guanajuato, according to Orlando-based non-profit Colectivo Árbol. Officials have yet to confirm his identity.

Isaret Jeffers, who represents the organization and has been providing support to his wife, Jessica Alamilla, said Coronilla Duran arrived in the United States three weeks ago for vacation, and had only been in Florida for two days. He was hit and killed by the truck on July 14.

“He was going to return this past Saturday. He had already bought a flight,” Jeffers said. “Now, unfortunately, if he is returning, his return is different.”

The Florida Highway Patrol told the Miami Herald last week that the agency found he had been running from an encounter with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations agents. DHS has not provided new details since the incident took place last week.

His was the third death following an encounter with immigration officials in a week, after federal agents shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican man in Houston on July 7, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian man, in Biddeford, Maine on July 13. Neither of the men were the targets of the agents.

As the Trump Administration carries out a sweeping mass deportation campaign, agents are rounding up immigrants on sidewalks, highways and in homes, some with work permits and other legal documentation. U.S. citizens have also been stopped and detained.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has opened an investigation into the deaths of at least 18 Mexican nationals since Trump assumed office, some of whom died during arrests and others in immigration detention. She said her government wants to file criminal charges.

“We express our deepest solidarity and sincere condolences to the family of the victims. Their pain is shared by the entire nation,” Sheinbaum said on July 14. “No fellow citizen should be unprotected when facing possible abuse from authority, disproportionate use of force, or human rights violations.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security declined to provide further details of last week’s incident in St. Augustine.

“On July 14, DHS law enforcement conducted an operation near St. Johns, Florida. Florida Highway Patrol and HSI are investigating an incident resulting in the death of a Mexican national,” read a statement sent again to the Herald on Monday. “We will provide an update when available.”

Coronilla Duran’s wife found out about his death while watching television, Jeffers said. Alamilla declined a request to be interviewed, and Jeffers said she is focused on returning home with his body.

Alamilla hadn’t heard from her husband in more than a day when she saw the news that a man had been killed, and feared it was him. The couple have been married for 10 years and have a seven-month-old daughter and a seven-year-old son, Jeffers said. They own a small business in San Luis de La Paz.

Alamilla flew to Florida on Friday to make arrangements with a local funeral home, Jeffers said, while relatives watched their children. On Monday, she worked with the Mexican consulate to take his body back home to Mexico.

Of the Mexicans who have died in ICE custody or during arrests, at least four died by presumed suicide, including 19-year-old Royer Perez-Jimenez in March in Florida.

Jeffers said that Colectivo Árbol mainly supports farmworkers, many of whom are afraid to leave their homes amid immigration arrests.

“People are too afraid to go out and do things that used to be normal, like going to the supermarket, taking their kids to the park,” Jeffers said. “None of that is happening anymore.”

Unmarked blue SUVs

Jose Rivera, a truck driver for a garbage collection company, witnessed Coronilla Duran run out of the gas station in front of a Wawa convenience store off the highway.

Rivera had stopped for breakfast, and was sitting in his truck parallel to the highway just before 7 a.m. Coronilla Duran wore a light sky blue hoodie over a white T-shirt, blue jeans and Timberland shoes, he said.

Coronilla Duran ran to the sidewalk leading to State Road 16 and turned around. Rivera followed Coronilla Duran’s gaze in his truck’s rearview mirror to see what he was running from.

“That’s when I see the undercover car with the lights on,” Rivera said. “But when I looked back, he started running across the road.”

Rivera said he saw unmarked blue SUVs with tinted windows stopped on either side of a car at the gas station, and one moved to follow Coronilla Duran. The agents were in green uniforms, he said, and he thought they were from St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office. But the sheriff’s office told the Herald it wasn’t involved in the incident, and responded later to investigate the traffic accident.

Rivera said Coronilla Duran reached the median of the highway, a small strip of grass, slipped and fell, picked himself up, and stumbled onto the asphalt of the other lane of traffic.

“The traffic was coming pretty quick, and he just lost his footing and didn’t look where the traffic was coming,” Rivera said. “He kept looking back.”

Rivera watched as the man fell in front of a trailer-tractor, and knew instantly that he had died.

Agents didn’t notice at first, Rivera thought, because he saw an officer point to the woods on the other side, as if they thought he escaped. But then they noticed the body in the road.

“It was a heartbreaking moment for me,” Rivera said. “I have kids around his age.”

Officers began to close off the road, and Rivera drove off. When he later heard the man’s age he found it hard to believe. He looked younger, in the brief second Rivera glimpsed his face.

“I hate when things like that happen, especially to young ones,” Rivera told the Herald. “I’m almost 60, and yeah, you know, I’ve been through a lot of life, but everybody should make it until they’re older, right?”

text:
This is the first time that the Strasbourg Court has agreed to examine an application concerning events that took place at an Immigration Detention Centre in Spain.

Barcelona, 21 July 2026. – The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) has communicated to the Spanish Government an application lodged by Irídia on behalf of the victim concerning the assaults and ill-treatment reported by an individual while being held at Barcelona’s Immigration Detention Centre (CIE), as well as the Spanish authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation into the events.

The communication of the application means that the Strasbourg Court will examine the case and that the Spanish State must now provide explanations regarding the shortcomings in the investigation of this particular case and, more broadly, the protocols in place to prevent ill-treatment in immigration detention centres.

The application argues that the Spanish authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation following a complaint of torture. Among other shortcomings, the detention centre failed to properly preserve the CCTV footage, meaning that it could not be recovered when the judge ordered its disclosure. Furthermore, the complainant was expelled from the country before he was able to give evidence about the events.

The complainant was subsequently able to return to Spain and give evidence before the authorities, at which point he fully reaffirmed his complaint. He also underwent a forensic medical examination, which confirmed both the existence of erythema consistent with the reported assault and psychological after-effects linked to the events. Despite this evidence, the Spanish courts refused to bring the case to trial.

For Irídia, the ECtHR’s decision is particularly significant because it will allow the Court to examine the State’s obligations to protect people deprived of their liberty and to investigate any allegation of torture or ill-treatment rigorously, independently and effectively.

This obligation is particularly important in immigration detention centres, where people are deprived of their liberty, placed in a situation of particular vulnerability and held under the direct custody of the State.

As Irídia has been denouncing for many years, immigration detention centres are spaces where rights and legal safeguards are effectively suspended. This is not only because they involve the deprivation of liberty on strictly administrative grounds linked to public border-control policies, but also because they lack genuine and effective mechanisms for preventing torture. In recent years, Irídia has identified numerous structural obstacles in the process of reporting ill-treatment at Barcelona’s Immigration Detention Centre, preventing detainees from accessing justice on equal terms with the rest of the population.

Irídia hopes that the proceedings before the Strasbourg Court will help strengthen the protection of fundamental rights in immigration detention centres, improve the mechanisms for preventing and investigating ill-treatment, and ensure that situations such as the one reported do not go unpunished.

text:
A Boston district court judge has blocked Trump administration policies that threatened to push immigrant workers out of jobs beginning this week.

Judge Nathaniel Gorton granted a stay barring retroactive application of new time limits on work permits and asylum fees added in a 2025 law until at least Aug. 5.

That pause reflects the potentially severe consequences faced by plaintiffs, rather than a consideration of the merits, he said in an order Tuesday for the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts.

The Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts argued in a lawsuit filed this month that US Citizenship and Immigration Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act by imposing provisions of a sweeping Republican tax and spending package (H.R. 1) on asylum seekers and Temporary Protected Status holders with benefit requests pending when the law took effect.

USCIS regulations capped the duration of employment authorization documents at one year for TPS holders, including those previously extended by 540 days based on automatic grace periods rescinded by the Trump administration. The agency also mandated that asylum seekers pay a new $100 annual fee to have claims considered.

TPS holders would have begun to see their work permits expire Wednesday, Gorton noted. His order means immigrants’ work permits will keep their prior expiration dates. He also stayed policies to reject asylum applications, terminate work authorization, and begin removal proceedings over failure to pay the annual asylum fee.

Gorton ruled the government could continue charging an annual asylum fee, and said it didn’t need to abide by a previous 30-day timeline for processing initial work permit requests for asylum seekers.

USCIS reinstated that timeframe for work permits Monday, saying it had inadvertently removed it from an April 29 interim final rule.

“The court’s ruling ensures that thousands of families will not lose their livelihoods and their peace of mind while the courts consider the legality of these policies,” said Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, which represents the plaintiffs.

Plaintiffs are also represented by the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project and the National Day Laborer Organizing Network. The government is represented by the Department of Justice.

title: Man detained by ICE believes his advocacy for Palestinian rights made him a target - NPR
description:
SALAH SARSOUR: I saw this man, young man, coming toward me.
And immediately he approached me saying, are you Salah Sarsour?
SARSOUR: One of them identified himself with badge saying, Salah Sarsour, you're under arrest - I'm with ICE.
FADEL: Sarsour was born in Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
FADEL: Salah Sarsour is the president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee.
text:
Transcript

LEILA FADEL, HOST:

On March 30, Salah Sarsour started his day in Franklin, Wisconsin, planning to take his mom to the doctor. But when he walked out of the house, it became clear the day had other plans for him.

SALAH SARSOUR: I saw this man, young man, coming toward me. And I saw, like, kind of a large gun next to him.

FADEL: (Gasping).

SARSOUR: I was kind of surprised - what's going on? And immediately he approached me saying, are you Salah Sarsour?

FADEL: Soon, Sarsour says there were about a dozen cars parked in front of him. Some 20 officers got out of those cars.

SARSOUR: One of them identified himself with badge saying, Salah Sarsour, you're under arrest - I'm with ICE.

FADEL: He was sure it had to be a mistake. He lived in the United States for over 30 years, has had a green card for most of that time. He's a respected leader at one of the largest mosques in Wisconsin and has a pristine record. He's also known in his community for his advocacy for Palestinian rights. And that advocacy, he says, is why the government is targeting him.

SARSOUR: For me, it's very obvious. It's just because my activism and my stand with human rights and just causes, especially the cause of Palestine.

FADEL: His lawyers say it's part of a trend by the government that started with the detention of college students last year who'd protested the war in Gaza. Sarsour was detained for 80 days, where he says he faced religious discrimination.

SARSOUR: I requested for at least a prayer mat to have something clean under me when I pray, and they don't give me anything. Then I requested a Quran, and they don't have a Quran. They not allow us Muslim at all, till I left, to gather as Muslims and pray the Friday prayer, while they're allowing Christians and other religion to gather and to do the weekly prayer together. I request to use the same rules for Muslims, and they refused.

FADEL: Last month, a Trump-appointed federal judge ordered Sarsour's release. The judge said Sarsour had raised a, quote, "substantial" First Amendment retaliation claim, and that Sarsour's speech on Palestinian rights is protected.

SARSOUR: He gave me hope in the system. This judge make me feel, wait a minute, there's still righteous people. There are still fair people here in the system.

FADEL: Sarsour was born in Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. And his experiences as a teenager, that the government has long known about, are now part of the U.S. government's case to detain and eventually deport him.

The Department of Homeland Security has called you a, quote, "terrorist." They've pointed to two Israeli military court convictions. One for throwing Molotov cocktails and stones at the home of Israeli armed forces in 1989, and another in 1995, where you were convicted for attempting to hold weapons and ammunition. How do you respond to those accusations, the things they're calling you?

SARSOUR: So I was arrested when I was 15 years old or 15 1/2 from my house in Al-Bireh, Ramallah. The Israeli soldiers came to my house with weapons, and they arrested me as a child. From my house, they took me to the Israeli bad news prison there. And I went through full torture, actually. Even they threatened me with rape. Now, even the document they made us sign, like, as a child - imagine, 15 years old.

FADEL: Yeah.

SARSOUR: They make me sign a document in Hebrew language. I don't understand a word of it. And right now, to be honest with you, I don't know what I signed in that year, 1988. After that, the judge kept me in prison for 23 months. And even the American government and the American embassy, they learned about my situation. That's why they gave me a waiver, and they gave me the green card, because they understood that I went through this tough situation in my childhood. It's not like something secret.

FADEL: Yeah, I mean, that's in your court documents. Actually, in the judge's decision to release you, he mentions that the United States government had been aware of these charges against Mr. Sarsour for 25 years, having considered them in 2000, 2008, 2010 and 2019 in evaluating Mr. Sarsour's eligibility for naturalization. For people who don't understand, the Israeli military courts try Palestinian civilians in areas that are Israeli-military-controlled, correct? Under occupation.

SARSOUR: Hundred percent.

FADEL: And human rights groups have documented abuses of the system, limited due process. And this has really faced scrutiny. Israel has defended the process. DHS also accused you of lying on your green card application. What do you say to that?

SARSOUR: I explained this point with immigration in many meetings. There's a question if I did any crime. And I wrote, no, I don't do any crime in the States. I have a very clean record in the States.

FADEL: Right.

SARSOUR: I'm a businessman, family man and a community person. So they wrote it now as if I supposed to say, no, however, I did or I went through what I went through in Palestine...

FADEL: Yeah.

SARSOUR: ...Under the Israeli occupation. I don't have nothing to hide. I want to show the entire world, like, as children, what we go through under the occupation. So they consider it lie. I don't know how it's lie and I'm still fighting this.

FADEL: Now, Salah Sarsour is back home with his family, which includes six children and nine grandchildren. During our interview, you could hear one of his youngest grandchildren trying to get his attention.

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Laughter).

SARSOUR: They're so attached to me.

FADEL: Oh, they are?

SARSOUR: It's like I'm trying to run away from them. I don't know where their mom gone.

FADEL: He says returning to his community, his family has renewed his strength.

SARSOUR: I'm going to continue the fight for the future, again, of my children and to continue what I'm doing in my community. I mean, with the support I have and love I have, I want to just continue the fight until, hopefully, justice will prevail and this case will end in the right direction.

FADEL: Salah Sarsour is the president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee. He's a father, a grandfather and a community leader in Wisconsin. Thank you for speaking with us. I appreciate your time.

SARSOUR: Thank you very much, Leila. I really appreciate it.

(SOUNDBITE OF THE SOUND DEFECTS' "PLAN B")

FADEL: We reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for a response to what Salah Sarsour said about his treatment in detention. A DHS spokesperson wrote in part, quote, "any accusation of discrimination by ICE agents is false." They also wrote, thanks to this court order, this public safety threat is now loose on our streets. We also reached out to the Israel prison service to ask about Sarsour's account of torture and being forced to sign a confession in a language he didn't understand. We have not heard back. Sarsour's next immigration hearing is scheduled for Wednesday.

text:
House Plan to Pass Anti-Children, Anti-Family, and Anti-Asylum H.R. 9773 Is Abdication of Congress’ Commitment to Freedom

Over 100 national, state, and local groups call on Congress to uniformly reject HR 9773

After writing a historic blank check to ICE and Border Patrol to further assault our communities, the Trump administration’s allies in Congress are eyeing their next target: children and people fleeing for their lives. The House Judiciary Committee is moving to mark up a new version of H.R.2, a bill anti-immigrant members of Congress first introduced in 2023 to spread fear of a “mass invasion” by immigrants, pit American citizens against their immigrant neighbors, and scapegoat them for the nation’s problems. If passed, this bill would codify the most extreme anti-asylum and anti-children policies in modern American history.

While wrongly touted as a “border security” bill, HR 9773 would have disastrous consequences for people who live here. The bill creates arbitrary penalties to criminalize longtime community members who will suddenly face deportation, when combined with the recent policy aimed at severely restricting the ability for people to gain permanent status in the United States. This will lead to families being separated, chaos in our work force, and an expansion of immigration detention and deportation for longtime residents, including those pushed out of status due to U.S. bureaucratic delays.

The bill would also turbocharge the administration’s cruelty to kids and people fleeing violence abroad by eviscerating landmark protections passed under the bipartisan Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act and decimating the Flores Settlement. This cruelty knows no end. Already, approximately 205,000 children have been separated from their parents due to mass detention and deportation in the past 18 months – leading to hundreds of children being redetained, placed into foster care, and facing life-threatening risks or death after their parents’ rushed deportations. This administration has created new rules to coerce unaccompanied children, including trafficking survivors, to abandon their claims and “self-deport”, and put kids in mass deportation tribunals without legal counsel. It is holding children and families in prolonged detention with insufficient medical care in violation of the Flores Settlement, creating life-long trauma for numerous children, including many who are Indigenous.

This bill tramples on asylum protections passed by Congress over 45 years ago, just as the world prepares to celebrate the 75th anniversary of most nations committing to protect the right to refuge. While our immigration system needs to be modernized to respond to modern migration challenges, this bill does nothing to accomplish that. Instead, it decimates asylum – a life-saving protection for people who are survivors of torture and gender-based violence, outspoken opponents of brutal dictatorships, LGBTQ+ individuals, religious advocates persecuted for their faith, Indigenous Peoples and individuals facing racial violence, among other at-risk groups. Already, this administration has shut down asylum processing across the Southern border and deported hundreds to torture prisons. Tens of thousands of people, including some who have judicial orders of protection based on refugee claims, have been sent to third countries to which they have no connection and where they face arbitrary detention, torture, and even onward refoulement to their country of persecution. This bill would compound these harms and expel asylum seekers from local economies – spiraling the already devastating job loss ushered in by this administration’s mass deportation policies.

This is not a border security bill; it is a bill to codify and accelerate attacks on lawful immigration, longtime residents, vulnerable children, and people seeking refuge. It will subject potentially millions of our neighbors and hard-working families to ICE’s inhumane, deadly, and lawless prisons.

Every member of Congress should rise in opposition of H.R. 9773 and recommit the United States to protect the rights of our immigrant neighbors, children, and people seeking refuge.

text:
SAN FRANCISCO -- A man says he was offended and shocked after a United Airlines employee at San Francisco International Airport suggested calling U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on him during a confrontation over a ticketing issue.

Julio Varela said the incident happened last Tuesday after he spent about three hours trying to correct a ticketing error for his daughter before a family trip to Montreal.

According to Varela, he, his wife and their two daughters were attempting to fly to Montreal on July 14 when they discovered one daughter's ticket had her middle and last names mixed up.

He said the error sent the family back and forth between United Airlines and Air Canada counters for hours.

Varela said an Air Canada employee was working to resolve the issue when a United employee joined the conversation.

"She said 'I already told you. I can't do anything. Whether you fly out or not, I don't care,'" Varela said. "That's what triggered me to say, 'you're rude.' And I also said you're rude and you're lazy."

Varela said he then took out his cellphone and asked the employee for her name.

Both he and the employee recorded the interaction.

In video of the confrontation, the employee can be heard saying: "Maybe we should call ICE on you."

When Varela responded, "You going to call ICE on me," the employee continued: "Maybe you need to be. Because you don't act like a citizen."

We have blurred the employee's face in video of the exchange.

Varela said the comment escalated the dispute.

"That's obviously when I lost it even more because I was already angered and bothered angered by the way she didn't care."

He said the remark was particularly upsetting.

"My jaw dropped. Number one. I was shocked and immediately I was angry," Varela said.

Varela, who identified himself as Hispanic and Mexican, said he was especially troubled by the employee's reference to ICE.

"If she is going to have the gall to say 'I'm going to call ICE' on a Hispanic person, Mexican, and to say that in San Francisco..."

He said the comment was especially concerning amid recent public attention surrounding immigration enforcement actions.

In a statement, United Airlines said: "We're looking into the interaction in this video, but don't have anything additional to share at this time."

Varela said he was not surprised by the airline's response.

He said a United representative contacted him to get his account of what happened and that the two sides communicated briefly by email.

However, Varela said the airline later stopped contacting him.

United has not provided additional details about the incident.

text:
Washington, DC – Today, Congressman Bill Foster (D-IL) introduced the Protecting Immigrants from Legal Exploitation Act. The legislation would create penalties for those who provide fraudulent immigration legal services and allow immigrants who are victims of fraud to have their cases reconsidered under certain circumstances. It would also create grant programs to educate immigrants on how to avoid legal service fraud and help qualified nonprofit organizations provide legal services to immigrants.

In many Latin American countries, "notario" or "notario público" refers to state-appointed lawyers. However, in the United States, a notary only has the authority to witness and certify legal documents. This linguistic discrepancy can expose many recent immigrants, particularly those from Latin American countries, to the risk of fraudulent immigration legal services.

“My office, like many other Members of Congress, has seen a large increase in people seeking assistance with their immigration cases in the wake of the Trump Administration’s attacks on immigrant communities,” said Rep. Foster. “Now more than ever, well-meaning immigrants are vulnerable to fraudulent immigration lawyers looking to exploit them for money, possibly leading to their deportation. It's time to stop scammers from targeting vulnerable immigrants who are working to follow the legal immigration process in a time of fear and uncertainty.”

The Protecting Immigrants from Legal Exploitation Act is cosponsored by Reps. Salud Carbajal (D-CA), Judy Chu (D-CA), Gil Cisneros (D-CA), Yvette Clarke (D-NY), Jesús “Chuy” García (D-IL), Hank Johnson (D-GA), Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), Jim McGovern (D-MA), Seth Moulton (D-MA), Jerrold Nadler (D-NY), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-DC), Jimmy Panetta (D-CA), Mike Quigley (D-IL), Jan Schakowsky (D-IL), Paul Tonko (D-NY), Juan Vargas (D-CA), and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-FL).

title: Attacks on human dignity can never be normalized, say 2 US bishops after deadly ICE shootings
description:
(OSV News) — Two U.S. Catholic bishops are lamenting recent deadly immigration enforcement encounters, calling for God-given human dignity to be respected in every individual.
On July 14, ICE agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian, after being stopped by ICE agents near a laundromat.
The Trump administration briefly halted, then resumed, ICE traffic stops in the wake of the deaths.
“ “Our pastoral concerns are distinct from what the civil law itself may permit,” said the two bishops.
In a report released in June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights counted 52 deaths in ICE custody during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration.
text:
(OSV News) — Two U.S. Catholic bishops are lamenting recent deadly immigration enforcement encounters, calling for God-given human dignity to be respected in every individual.

“As Catholics, we believe that all persons are created in the image and likeness of God and, therefore, grieve all situations where human life is brought to an unnatural end. This is a core teaching of our faith and one we can never grow weary of proclaiming as disciples of Our Lord Jesus Christ,” said Bishop Daniel E. Garcia of Austin, Texas, and Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Victoria, Texas.

The two issued a July 20 joint pastoral reflection as chairs, respectively, of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ Subcommittee for the Promotion of Racial Justice and Reconciliation and the USCCB’s Committee on Migration.

Their statement follows three separate deaths recorded days apart in July amid operations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers as they implement the Trump administration’s hardline crackdown on immigration.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Houston area man, was fatally shot en route to work in his vehicle July 7 during an ICE traffic stop. On July 14, ICE agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian, after being stopped by ICE agents near a laundromat. Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, a 28-year-old man from Mexico, was struck and killed by a tractor trailer July 15 in St. Augustine, Florida, while fleeing ICE and Homeland Security agents on foot.

ICE’s claims that Salgado and Durán attempted to ram officials with their respective vehicles have been disputed, with Houston law enforcement officials expressing frustration over the federal agency’s lack of collaboration in investigating forensic evidence in Salgado’s death.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that Salgado — a Mexican national who had been in the U.S. for some 35 years, and who was in the process of obtaining legal authorization to reside and work in the country — was not the intended target of the ICE operation in which he died.

In Colorado, an employee of the GEO Group — a private firm that contracts with ICE to operate its Aurora processing center — opened fire July 16 on a protester at the site, injuring the woman’s foot.

The Trump administration briefly halted, then resumed, ICE traffic stops in the wake of the deaths.

In their statement, Bishops Garcia and Cahill quoted from the USCCB’s November 2025 special pastoral message on immigration: “We are disturbed when we see among our people a climate of fear and anxiety around questions of profiling and immigration enforcement.”

Drawing on the USCCB’s 2018 pastoral letter on racism, “Open Wide Our Hearts,” the bishops stressed that “racial profiling in particular violates God-given dignity,” adding the practice “also inflicts profound harm on individuals, families, and communities by fostering fear, eroding trust, and increasing the risk of unjust and even tragic outcomes. “

“Our pastoral concerns are distinct from what the civil law itself may permit,” said the two bishops.

They warned that “acts that diminish or disregard the dignity of any person or group of people should never be normalized in our society,” pointing to both “the dehumanization of immigrants, regardless of their legal status” and “the vilification of law enforcement officers” as examples.

Bishops Garcia and Cahill said they “continue to affirm the legitimate role of civil authorities to implement the law in a humane manner and with respect for fundamental human rights, including the rights to life and due process.”

Underscoring that “the power of the state must always be exercised within the limits of the moral law,” they called for “accountability, transparency, and justice, which require that meaningful reforms be made to our immigration system.”

The bishops said they “join in praying for the souls of those killed and for their families, for our nation, and for all those entrusted with the duties of public service.”

They also prayed “for an end to dehumanizing rhetoric, racial prejudice, and violence and for a renewed commitment to recognizing the inherent dignity of every person as a child of God,” and pleaded for “the intercession of Mary, Our Mother, who is the model of perfect faith in times of grief, hardship, and uncertainty.”

According to data analyzed by The Guardian, eight persons — including U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti — have been shot to death by federal immigration agents under the current Trump administration as of July 15, with 13 injured and another 9 other shooting incidents with no injuries.

In a report released in June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights counted 52 deaths in ICE custody during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration. The two organizations said ICE “fails to disclose adequate information about the circumstances surrounding deaths in its custody,” with medical neglect suspected as a key factor.

As of April, more than 60,000 are in ICE custody, the majority of whom (just under 71%) have no criminal convictions, according to Syracuse University’s Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

text:
Boston — A federal court today granted emergency relief preventing the federal government from implementing unlawful U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) policies that threatened to strip tens of thousands of asylum seekers and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders of work authorization, and to prevent otherwise eligible individuals from pursuing asylum.

The ruling, which will remain in effect while this case proceeds, comes the day before thousands of TPS holders faced the imminent loss of their employment authorization under USCIS policies implementing portions of the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Without emergency intervention, many TPS holders would have been unable to work beginning July 22, and asylum seekers faced rejection of their asylum applications and immediate termination of their work authorization.

The lawsuit, filed by the Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts, the National TPS Alliance, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project (ASAP), the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), and 32BJ SEIU, challenges USCIS policies that unlawfully impose new barriers on asylum seekers and TPS holders, including policies that threaten to reject asylum applications and terminate work authorization without adequate notice or due process, and unlawfully shorten employment authorization for TPS recipients.

Plaintiffs are represented by Democracy Forward, the National Day Laborer Organizing Network, and ASAP.

The coalition and co-counsel issued the following statement:

“This decision protects thousands of asylum seekers and TPS holders from immediate and irreparable harm while this case moves forward. Without this relief, families who have followed the law and relied on longstanding humanitarian protections faced the sudden loss of their employment authorization and ability to support themselves through no fault of their own. Asylum seekers also faced rejection of their applications for relief. The order provides protections while the court considers the serious legal questions presented in this case. We remain committed to ensuring that people seeking safety and those protected by TPS receive the lawful process Congress guaranteed and that these unlawful policies are permanently set aside.”

The case is Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts et al. v. USCIS et al.; the legal team at Democracy Forward includes Sean Ouellette, Jennie Kneedler, Steven Bressler, and Brian Netter.

text:
[Episcopal News Service] Episcopal leaders are offering support for Haitian immigrants in their communities while calling on Congress to help protect them from deportation after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end federal protections.

In Springfield, Ohio, which became a flashpoint during the 2024 presidential campaign over the city’s growing Haitian migrant community, some Haitian families had begun attending worship services at Christ Episcopal Church. The Rev. Michelle Boomgaard told Episcopal News Service that attendance noticeably declined after the Supreme Court’s June 25 ruling.

Some Haitians already had legal residency through other federal programs. Others have begun applying for asylum or green cards, which should again provide them with at least temporary protection from deportation, Boomgaard said, as returning to their home country isn’t a safe option. “At the end of the day, the situation in Haiti has not improved.”

More than 300,000 Haitians had been allowed to live and work in the United States for years under a program known as Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, that has long been supported by The Episcopal Church. It allows the Department of Homeland Security to declare certain foreign nationals protected from deportation if they would face hazards in their home countries from conditions such as natural disasters, civil unrest or other violence.

Those protections were thrown into limbo when the Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump’s history of racist and discriminatory statements toward Haitians and other immigrants did not negate the presidential authority to end TPS protections for those immigrants. The ruling also directly affects a small group of Syrians, and it could make it easier for the Trump administration to roll back TPS for immigrants from 10 other countries.

The Episcopal Church’s Washington, D.C.-based Office of Government Relations released a statement on the day of the ruling, lamenting that “families who have built their lives, raised children, worshiped, worked and contributed to their communities in the United States may now face the loss of work authorization and protection from deportation.”

On July 16, the Office of Government Relations’ Episcopal Public Policy Network followed up with an action alert calling on Episcopalians to urge their representatives in Congress to enact legislative protections for Haitian families. It warned that Haiti “continues to face a profound humanitarian and security crisis” with “widespread violence, kidnapping, political instability, and limited access to basic services.”

“Conditions remain so dire that many advocates, faith leaders, and humanitarian organizations have warned that there is no realistic opportunity for a safe and orderly return for Haitian nationals at this time,” the action alert said.

On July 2, New York Bishop Matthew Heyd joined a grew of faith leaders in speaking in support of TPS a vigil outside a federal building in Manhattan. In addition, a group of about 20 Episcopal bishops launched a letter-writing campaign this month calling on Senate leaders and the Department of Homeland Security to renew TPS for Haitians.

“They are our friends, they are our neighbors, they are our congregants, they are our clergy,” Massachusetts Bishop Julia Whitworth said July 20 in a Facebook video about the bishops’ effort. “This is personal, and it’s urgent.”

General Convention has long supported immigration policies that treat migrants with dignity. In 2015, it approved a resolution pledging to support Temporary Protected Status “for all immigrants fleeing for refuge from violence, environmental disaster, economic devastation, or cultural abuse or other forms of abuse.”

The Diocese of Haiti is part of The Episcopal Church’s Province II, and Haitian immigrant communities in some American cities have grown large enough to support sizable Episcopal congregations, like St. Paul’s et Les Martyrs d’Haiti in Miami, Florida, and the Haitian Congregation of the Good Samaritan in New York City. In Elizabeth, New Jersey, Haitians helped revive the dwindling congregation of St. Elizabeth’s Episcopal Church, according to a Religion News Service report, though fear of federal immigration authorities this year has kept many families away.

When Trump first took office in 2017, his administration tried to end protections for many of those with TPS, saying the status never was intended to offer immigrants permanent residency.

Then during the 2024 presidential campaign, Trump specifically targeted the growing Haitian community in Springfield, Ohio, using dehumanizing and false rhetoric about Springfield residents eating pets. After returning to office in January 2025, Trump has prioritized sharp reductions of both legal and illegal immigration and now is following through on efforts to end TPS for Haitians and other immigrant groups.

An estimated 15,000 Haitian migrants had moved to Springfield since 2020, seeking jobs that local leaders were desperate to fill in the city’s ongoing effort to reverse decades of economic decline. In a small city with a population of less than 60,000, that sudden influx of new residents strained resources and services, though a network of Springfield organizations, including Christ Episcopal Church, coordinated efforts to better welcome these newest neighbors and ease their transition into the local community.

Since the Trump campaign’s attacks on those Haitian migrants, “folks in Springfield definitely feel like they have a target on their backs,” the Rev. Michelle Boomgaard, rector of Christ Episcopal Church, told Episcopal News Service in an interview this month. Now, the church and other community groups are scrambling to assist those who fear deportations after losing TPS.

“These are human beings and neighbors and friends and people we wave and say ‘hi’ to,” she said.

text:
YORK COUNTY, Va. (WAVY) — A video showing possible ICE activity in Yorktown is making the rounds, with residents in the Rose Hill neighborhood saying they watched as possible federal agents in unmarked cars chased several people Monday morning.

This comes amid confusion about the Department Of Homeland Security’s latest directive, which was supposed to halt most vehicle pursuits and traffic stops.

A veteran couple told 10 On Your Side they were startled by what they witnessed in their neighborhood Monday morning.

“It’s a normal day,” said Amanda Marie Tejada. “Workers are out here working. We’re going on a walk and then we just hear a lot of commotion.”

Tejada was referring to a chase that happened in the Rose Hill neighborhood in Yorktown.

What was a quiet walk with her husband took a frightening turn when they were stopped in their tracks at the sight. A video showed the moment at least one person ran into the woods after being chased by authorities in unmarked cars.

“You can see guys just running into the trees running screaming,” Tejada said. “I’m still just in shock.”

She took a photo of at least one person being detained. Tejada said she believes some of the people detained are possible construction workers who helped build the newly-constructed homes in the neighborhood.

“Immigrants built my beautiful home,” Tejada said.

As a veteran, she said there’s not much that rattles her, but this situation did. She was shocked to see the pursuit and its alarming speed, especially after the Department Of Homeland Security ordered ICE officers to stop pursuing people in vehicles after recent fatal shootings. That was issued last Tuesday.

The following day President Donald Trump opposed the directive and said that ICE agents should continue the pursuits. It’s still unclear exactly what ICE officers are to do regarding chases like these. Border Czar Tom Homan said agents may start wearing more body cameras.

10 On Your Side reached out to immigration officials to learn exactly about what happened in York County. We have yet to hear back.

“My neighbors’ kids ride their bikes this early in the morning,” Tejada said. “I go for walks with my kids. … Now, every time a car goes by, I’m like, who is that, what’s going to happen?”

She said many are living with a high level of fear.

“This can’t be the America we live in,” Tejada said. “I can’t protect my children from seeing that, or from getting ran over. They could’ve ran over one of the workers. I don’t want this for immigrants coming to America. They are trying to do the best they can for their families. There’s a humane way to go about this.”

text:
The Supreme Court may have crushed President Trump’s plans to restrict birthright citizenship, but congressional Republicans are seeking legislative alternatives that could restrict it in certain cases.

Some of the bills seek to maneuver at the edges of the high court’s ruling, clamping down on women who enter the U.S. on legal visas to engage in “birth tourism” or stripping automatic citizenship from children born to noncitizens in U.S. territories, such as Puerto Rico.

Other legislation amounts to a frontal attack on the justices’ reasoning by attempting to establish Congress’ right to define citizenship.

The result is a cottage industry in birthright bills.

“The Supreme Court’s birthright citizenship decision was an unprecedented assault on American sovereignty, and we must do whatever it takes to save our country,” said Sen. Jim Banks, Indiana Republican, who is sponsoring one of the bills to push back on the court’s ruling.

In the June 30 ruling, five Supreme Court justices held that the Constitution’s 14th Amendment guarantees automatic citizenship to nearly every child born on U.S. soil, including those born to illegal immigrants or temporary visitors. A sixth justice, Brett M. Kavanaugh, voted to strike down the order on separate statutory grounds.

That decision was authored by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. and joined by Justice Amy Coney Barrett, a fellow Republican appointee, and the court’s three Democratic appointees: Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.

Justice Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee, ruled against the president on the basis of the Nationality Act of 1940, which explicitly granted automatic citizenship. He disagreed that the Constitution forbade Mr. Trump’s policy.

Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Neil M. Gorsuch dissented in the case, known as Trump v. Barbara.

Sen. Eric Schmitt, Missouri Republican, called for a frontal attack on the court’s ruling.

His legislation would rewrite the Immigration and Nationality Act to explicitly declare that children of illegal immigrants and temporary visitors do not qualify for automatic citizenship. Mr. Schmitt has also proposed a constitutional amendment addressing birthright citizenship.

“It would restart our fight in the courts for sanity in birthright citizenship. While the Supreme Court’s decision threatens to destroy American citizenship, I am fighting to defend it,” he said.

Mr. Banks’ bill, meanwhile, is a complex legal attack. It would declare that illegal immigrants are “invaders” under federal law, then use one of the already recognized exceptions to birthright citizenship — children born to invading armies — and expand that to the children of the illegal immigrant “invasion.”

A group of Republican senators has written a bill to clamp down on birth tourism, explicitly declaring that foreigners who seek to come to the U.S. with the primary goal of delivering a child to earn citizenship can be barred from the country — and deported if already here.

Rep. Morgan Griffith, Virginia Republican, has written a bill that would strip citizenship from future children born to noncitizens in Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands. American Samoa, which does not confer automatic citizenship, is not covered by the bill. Congress has the power to write citizenship rules for the territories.

The debate is at the ideas stage, but Republican leaders have signaled interest.

“If there’s some legislative fix, we’ll advance that,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, Louisiana Republican, told “Fox News Sunday” after the high court’s ruling. “If it’s a constitutional amendment, as you know, it takes a little more time. But we’ve got to address this.”

Immigrant rights advocates are preparing their defenses, and congressional Democrats, in a series of speeches on the House floor last week, said they doubted the birthright fight is settled.

“History teaches us that constitutional rights are rarely lost all at once,” said Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Missouri Democrat. “They’re chipped away slowly, one exception, one excuse, one precedent at a time, until Americans wake up and discover that what once seemed guaranteed has quietly disappeared.”

Andrew “Art” Arthur, a former immigration judge and congressional staffer who wrote immigration legislation, said some of the Republicans’ narrow proposals are on firm footing.

He said Mr. Griffith’s bill about the territories falls firmly under Congress’ power to define who in the territories is a citizen.

He said Congress can try to restrict the entry of certain classes of migrants, including women coming to give birth for citizenship purposes. Indeed, the administration has already announced it will use existing tools to combat visa fraud.

The frontal attacks are tougher.

“The Supreme Court majority spoke fairly dispositively about that,” he said. “Anything that denies the child of illegal aliens who are here citizenship is probably going to run afoul of Barbara.”

He said Congress may have some latitude because the high court will give a congressional statute more deference than Mr. Trump’s executive order.

Mr. Arthur said there may be yet another way.

Part of the high court’s ruling relied on an interpretation of English common law, finding that children born on English soil were generally deemed to be subject to the king and thus entitled to citizenship.

Mr. Arthur said the formulation is odd to adopt for the U.S., which was founded explicitly to reject the authority of the king as sovereign.

He said Congress could pass legislation expressly stating that pre-independence common law would not apply to determinations of birthright citizenship. The justices would then have to confront whether Congress had that power.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Rand Paul (R-KY), Chairman of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, released documents showing that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) prepared a formal targeting action to question and search Peter Daszak, President of EcoHealth Alliance, upon his return to the United States from the World Health Organization’s investigation into the origins of COVID-19 — before the FBI intervened and asked agents to stand down.

The documents show CBP’s National Targeting Center flagged Daszak as “an extremely high person of interest” ahead of his February 5, 2021, arrival at JFK, citing his more than fifteen years of collaboration with the Wuhan Institute of Virology (WIV) and his role as principal investigator on NIH grants funding bat coronavirus research in China. Internal CBP records state that “much of the funding DASZAK receives is put towards gain of function research.”

CBP built out a formal targeting event and scheduled a Tactical Terrorism Response Team exam, with plans to question Daszak on his activities in China, his contacts at WIV, and whether he collected or carried biological samples.

Three days before his arrival, CBP received a request from the FBI’s New York Field Office: do not stop the subject. The inspection never took place.

The documents are now available to the public HERE and in The Reading Room at paul.senate.gov/readingroom.

title: United States: District Court Permits DHS to Move Forward With Yemen TPS Termination
description:
On July 20, a federal district court in the Southern District of New York lifted its earlier postponement order that blocked the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Yemen.

text:
On July 20, a federal district court in the Southern District of New York lifted its earlier postponement order that blocked the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Yemen. The district court’s new order permits DHS to move forward with its termination of Yemen TPS. Currently, the designation and related employment authorization documents (EAD) are scheduled to expire after July 24, 2026.

The district court action follows a June 25 U.S. Supreme Court decision, in which the Court ruled that the Trump Administration could proceed with its plan to terminate TPS designations for Haiti and Syria. In its June decision, the Supreme Court held that federal courts are not permitted to review TPS determinations by DHS on non-constitutional grounds and the Court rejected plaintiffs’ constitutional argument as a basis for postponing the Haiti TPS termination. Given that the same or similar arguments were made by plaintiffs in the Yemen TPS lawsuit, the district court found that it was bound by the Supreme Court decision, and lifted its earlier postponement order, permitting the Yemen TPS termination to move forward.

The district court case is Doe v. Noem, No. 1:26-cv-02280 (S.D.N.Y., filed March 19, 2026).

Yemen was first designated for TPS in 2015, and that designation had been repeatedly renewed, until this year, when DHS announced that TPS for Yemen would terminate on May 4, 2026. On May 1, the Doe district court issued an order postponing the termination, ruling that DHS failed to follow the statutorily mandated procedures for reviewing country conditions before making its decision to terminate the TPS designation.

On June 25, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a separate set of consolidated TPS cases that the Trump Administration could proceed with its plan to terminate the TPS designations for Haiti and Syria because the DHS decision to terminate a TPS designation was not reviewable by the courts. The Supreme Court decision is the basis for the Doe court’s July 20 order, and is anticipated to affect the outcome of all ongoing TPS litigation.

Since the Supreme Court decision was issued, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has been briefly extending the validity of TPS employment authorization documents (EADs) for several countries in short increments, including for Yemen.
