text:
Amna Nawaz:

Two fatal shootings this month involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have reignited protests and renewed questions about tactics, training and recruitment at the agency.

Both incidents took place during traffic stops, one in Maine and the other in Texas. None of the agents involved were wearing body cameras, and neither of the victims were the intended targets of the operation.

For more, we're joined now by John Sandweg. He's an attorney, and he served as acting director of ICE under President Barack Obama from 2013 to 2014.

John, welcome back. Thanks for being with us.

John Sandweg, Former Acting ICE Director:

Yes, thanks for having me.

Amna Nawaz:

So two men were killed in these latest stops. In Houston, Texas, it was 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, originally from Mexico. In Biddeford, Maine, it was 26-year-old Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, originally from Colombia.

In both cases, DHS has says the men attempted to flee and they weaponized their vehicles. From what we know, do the facts say to you that deadly force was justified here?

John Sandweg:

Amna, it's really difficult to tell based on the limited information we have available to us thus far.

But I think if you take a step back and you look at this trend, right, where we have at least 17 shootings involving ICE agents, not including other DA's officers, five of which have been fatal, it's clear to me we have a problem. And I think it's pretty easy, if you spent any time at ICE, understanding the source of the problem.

And that is how this administration is deploying these ICE agents and how we're using now vehicular stops as part of the tools that the ICE agents are using to effectuate these arrests.

I'll just say quickly, Amna, historically, traffic stops have never been a major part of ICE's operations. They don't need to be a major part of ICE's operations given that ICE can arrest the individual as they're getting in their car or after their car. And from a training perspective, because they weren't such a critical part of what ICE does, they've never been a major focus of training, like you'd see with other law enforcement agencies.

So, look, at the end of the day, I think that -- as you know, the secretary of DHS had recommended a pause. I think that made a lot of sense. We have a larger problem here. Regardless of whether any one of these shootings was individually justified, the trend itself is what's disturbing.

Amna Nawaz:

Well, the secretary recommended a pause, and the president intervened to say that those vehicular stops have to continue. So it doesn't seem like there will be a pause.

But I want to ask you about the body cameras in this as well, because none of the officers seem to be wearing them in these instances. We know ICE is flush with cash after some major funding bills, including $20 million dollars for body cameras specifically.

Why wouldn't those have been ruled out by now?

John Sandweg:

It's hard for me to say, right?

The administration, at least vocally, is saying that they're in favor of the body cameras. It certainly can't be, as you point out, money, right? I mean, the agency has tens of billions of dollars in the Big Beautiful Bill, tens more billions in this kind of two-year appropriation money that was recently given to them. So it's not a financial issue.

The only thing I could say is, it's a prioritization issue. And, Amna, if you go back at the history of the agency, I mean, it's probably fair to ask why weren't ICE agents wearing these already even before the Trump administration.

I think a lot of that, though, goes back to what I was talking about earlier, how ICE agents were being deployed. Historically, the vast majority of immigration arrests ICE makes are of individuals who are already in somebody else's custody.

And when you're taking -- or you're picking up someone at a local jail or you're going down to the Border Patrol station and picking them up at the border, it doesn't raise those same concerns that you have when you're deploying ICE agents to do these at-large arrests inside the communities, right? There, they're engaging with the public in a way where we need that body camera.

But, look, I know there have been excuses offered here about the shutdowns or this or that. Honestly, at the end of the day, it's just a prioritization issue. It just wasn't a priority. And I hope that now, in light of these incidents, it will be.

Amna Nawaz:

As you mentioned, we don't know a lot yet. So there are still many questions left unanswered.

But we do know a little bit about one of the officers reportedly involved in the Maine shooting, a man named David Brouillette. His ex-wife and several family members told the Associated Press he had a history of violence, that they believe he never should have had a badge or a gun.

His ex-wife, Ashley, actually told the AP that he called her, he acknowledged that he killed Duran Guerrero. And here's actually part of what she said about the encounter.

Ashley Brouillette, Ex-Wife of David Brouillette: I believe that this man was murdered. I believe that David -- David's mental health played a part in what happened. I think what happened was, he was standing there during that operation, had a PTSD moment and hit fight-or-flight mode. And, unfortunately, a man lost his life due to it.

Amna Nawaz:

Now, John, I want to be clear we don't know about this man's particular hiring circumstances, but there are questions about the vetting and the training of ICE agents in this hiring surge.

I want to play for you one more bit of sound, because our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, asked Tom Homan about that vetting process earlier today. Take a listen.

Liz Landers:

So you're satisfied with the training right now of ICE agents? Nothing needs to be improved?

Tom Homan, White House Border Czar:

There's always room for -- that's a loaded question. There's always room for improvement. Things change all the time. FBI updates their training. DEA updates their training. Every police department updates their training. But ICE used to -- look, I -- you can never be overtrained. I wish there was more training.

Amna Nawaz:

John, you ran this agency. Does all of this lead you to have concerns about the vetting and the training of the ICE agents?

John Sandweg:

Oh, absolutely.

I have real concerns here. This particular instant raises concerns about the vetting. As you indicated earlier, I don't know all the details of his background. And I'm not saying that there aren't circumstances by which someone like this could be hired, provided everything current -- their current state suggests they have the suitability to be a federal agent.

But it's incredibly rare for someone with that kind of background to be hired as a federal agent. And it raises real questions that, in this crazy push we're seeing to double the size of ICE, to recruit people, to cut short their training and get them deployed as quickly as possible, that we're dropping the ball in the vetting operation.

And really what concerns me is, if you look at what -- historically, ICE only hires a couple of hundred agents a year. And so the vetting offices were built to handle that volume.

And now we say to them, hey, you're going to hire 2,000, 3,000 people in a year, we want them vetted and onboarded as quickly as possible so we can get them on the streets as quickly as possible, it certainly makes you think, boy, there's a real chance here that, as they're building this thing on the fly, they're going to drop the ball on the vetting.

And, unfortunately, again, without knowing for sure whether this is a case of a dropped ball, the vetting was messed up here or something else going on, it absolutely raises concerns for me about, wow, are we failing to do a proper suitability check on these potential candidates, giving them -- minimizing their training, then putting them on the streets without knowing exactly who they are or what's in their background?

Amna Nawaz:

Hey, John, before I let you go, I want to ask you briefly about a bit of reporting from The New York Times, who looked at the hundreds of assault charges that the Trump administration has filed against people and protesters who come out to kind of record and protest some of the ICE crackdown.

They found, of the more than 400 cases that have been resolved so far, the administration lost nearly half. Defendants were acquitted or the cases unraveled. What does all of that say to you?

John Sandweg:

I think what it says to me, though, is, again, we have had this kind of -- you know, it makes me worry about the quality of the vetting before charging decisions were being made, right? We had this -- with this time period that I will give Secretary Mullin credit for, it seems to have dissipated, where you had ICE agents put in this position to aggressively confront these protesters.

I will say that, based on the shift in tactics thus far, that those incidents have gone down. But you saw a Justice Department that was quick to charge everyone and anyone, including in obviously in many of these cases, not necessarily all of them, many of these cases where there was flimsy evidence as to whether or not there was the intent to actually assault an officer or actually contact was made.

Look, I recognize that this situation, right, ICE -- ICE agents have an incredibly difficult job, and I do have a lot of sympathy for them. But this idea of kind of charging everything, even where the evidence doesn't support a federal criminal charge, doesn't do them any favors.

Amna Nawaz:

John Sandweg, always great to talk to you. Thank you so much for your time and perspective.

John Sandweg:

Thank you.

Jesus Espinosa, 52, of El Paso made his initial appearance in federal court after being indicted and then arrested, according to federal officials.

Prosecutors allege Espinosa claimed the person he detained was aggressive and non-compliant, which led to an erroneous official report of assault on a federal officer rather than a report detailing excessive use of force.

A Trump-nominated federal judge has ruled against the administration in a key case centered around local immigration policy in Minnesota.

According to a Monday filing, the Trump administration asserted that Minnesota sanctuary laws violate the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, which states that federal law must be supreme to state and local law. The administration looked to have the laws and policies declared unconstitutional and asked the court to block them, per the filing.

U.S. District Judge Eric C. Tostrud dismissed the case in his Monday ruling, writing that “the challenged provisions do not single the federal government out for less favorable treatment, at least not in any sense that shows an intergovernmental immunity violation.”

Earlier this year, Minnesota was at the center of controversy surrounding the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, with over 3,000 federal immigration personnel in the state at one point. Two U.S. citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Good, were killed in Minneapolis by federal immigration authorities in January, causing mass outrage.

ICE officers have also fatally shot multiple people in recent weeks, with two notable cases occurring in Texas and Maine.

In February, Tostrud held the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in civil contempt over violating a court order when it took a detainee to a facility in Texas the month prior. Tostrud ordered the federal government to compensate the detainee for a return flight to Minnesota.

Tostrud noted that the detainee, who is a Mexican citizen named Fernando, had been released from the Texas detainment facility in late January without his belongings. The judge argued that federal officials had yet to properly explain their actions.

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

text:
The U.S. Department of Justice sued the state of Maryland on Thursday over its in-state tuition policies for noncitizen students.

The department argued that Maryland’s policies discriminate against U.S. citizens and create incentives for illegal immigration into the country. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for Maryland, seeks an injunction to strike down the policies and to block Maryland from offering financial aid and scholarships to noncitizen students, the Justice Department said in a news release on Thursday regarding the lawsuit.

Under the 2011 Maryland DREAM Act, undocumented students can receive in-state tuition benefits if they graduated from a high school in the state and enroll in a public higher education institution within six years of receiving a high school diploma. The act also requires students or their parents to have filed a Maryland tax return for at least the past three years, and nonpermanent residents must pledge to file for permanent residency. In 2026, Maryland lawmakers reduced the requirement for income tax verification so that students needed to provide documentation that they or their family filed state taxes for just two years to receive the benefits.

[College Park’s Lidl temporarily closes until Aug. 5 for renovations]

The lawsuit states that federal law prohibits noncitizen students from receiving in-state tuition benefits if American students living outside of the state don’t also receive those benefits. It referenced a 2025 executive order from President Donald Trump that directs federal departments and agencies to “ensure, to the maximum extent permitted by law, that no taxpayer-funded benefits go to unqualified aliens.”

The Justice Department argued that undocumented students received preferential treatment over out-of-state U.S. citizens, as noncitizens collectively saved about $9 million in college tuition costs from in-state benefits between the summer of 2024 and spring of 2025, according to the lawsuit.

Maryland House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) wrote in a Thursday statement that the state’s tuition policy aims to give students who grew up and attended schools in Maryland access to higher education. This lawsuit is another example of the federal government asking the courts to override policies made by states through the democratic process, she wrote.

The lawsuit also names the University System of Maryland Board of Regents and the Maryland Higher Education Commission as defendants.

Michael Sandler, the university system’s vice chancellor for communications and marketing, declined to comment on pending litigation. A spokesperson for the Maryland Higher Education Commission did not respond to The Diamondback’s request for comment.

The lawsuit against Maryland comes amid a dozen others challenging other states’ over policies similarly providing in-state tuition benefits to undocumented students. Laws in Kentucky, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Texas have been struck down, according to the Justice Department news release, while lawsuits filed against eight other states await a decision.

Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown opposed the lawsuit in a Thursday statement, writing the Justice Department is suing to take away opportunities from Maryland students, who grew up and attended school in the state, to work towards a future for themselves and their families.

“We will respond through the courts, as we do whenever Maryland’s laws are challenged, and we will keep fighting for the young people in our state and their futures,” Brown’s statement read.

Sophomore government and politics major Cole Christesen said the lawsuit “seems entirely unfounded.” If noncitizen students living in Maryland pay state taxes, they should also “benefit off of the same benefits that they pay into,” he said.

[UMD students, faculty to gain access to IBM quantum computers through new partnership]

Christesen is a member of this university’s Young Democratic Socialists of America chapter, which launched a campaign in September urging this university to establish itself as a sanctuary campus and limit its cooperation with federal immigration enforcement agencies to protect immigrant and undocumented students.

The organization also launched a petition for the campaign demanding that this university reestablish the Immigrant and Undocumented Student Life office website, which provided resources for undocumented students about securing in-state tuition. The petition has over 3,100 signatures.

Resources from the webpage — which was taken down in the summer of 2025 — were integrated into this university’s Thrive Center for Essential Needs website, The Diamondback previously reported.

But the Thrive Center’s website is not the same.

Its website does not contain the words “immigrant” or “undocumented.” Many resources that were featured on the former Immigrant and Undocumented Student Life website are not located on the Thrive Center’s, which instead links to the university’s First-Gen Terps program. The previous website also provided resources to navigate residency reclassification under the Maryland DREAM Act, which the Thrive Center and First-Gen Terps pages do not.

“This is a policy that is available to all people who reside in the state of Maryland,” Christesen said. “Everyone has a right to higher education and that is also something that should be covered by taxpayers.”

text:
James Barnicle, the assistant director in charge of the FBI New York Field Office, said 43-year-old Andrew Arrabaca, a former United States Army soldier who served from 2001 to 2005, was responsible for the fiery attack on July 20 and had deadly intentions.

“He did say he was targeting the building, and he was okay if he hurt or killed people going in and out of the building, whether they were federal employees or civilians,” Barnicle told reporters during a press conference Monday afternoon.

Local and federal law enforcement report that Arrabaca drove in from Poughkeepsie and parked in Harlem on Sunday before sleeping on the street near the Holland Tunnel. He then arrived at immigration court around 5 a.m. Monday morning.

At approximately 8:30 a.m., law enforcement sources said, Arrabaca allegedly unleashed his attack by pouring gasoline over the street and igniting it using a firework. Once the inferno was lit, he brandished what is being described as an airsoft rifle and fired between five and seven shots.

Federal officers and a security guard for the building quickly tackled the gunman, placed him in handcuffs, and rushed him inside the building.

In addition to several fireworks, he also had two axes, a hammer, a machete, and three knives in his possession.

“On his cart … he had anti-ICE literature. When he was being arrested, he yelled derogatory terms to ICE, used bad words. Obviously, he is an anti-American, anti-government extremist. We know that from what he said. We know that from what he has said post-arrest, and we know that from the actions that he tried to take today,” Barnicle added.

amNewYork inquired if the FBI had knowledge of Arrabaca and if he had been spotted at any anti-ICE demonstrations. However, he said that federal authorities do not track protesters.

Meanwhile, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said that her department is supporting federal authorities in its investigation, and that charges have not yet been filed.

Still, law enforcement sources charged that the suspect’s intentions were clear — to destroy the building.

A small cart belonging to Arrabaca could be seen following his arrest, with the words “ICE off our streets” written on it. During the onslaught, three people were injured and one was hospitalized.

“There was a naturalization ceremony scheduled for today that was canceled, and the one civilian victim was an immigrant who had a hearing today for their immigration status. So that’s quite unfortunate, quite ironic at the same time,” Barnicle said.

For over a year, 26 Federal Plaza has become a symbol of ICE activity in the Big Apple after masked agents took people into custody, including mothers and fathers, following their legally mandated court hearings despite often not having any criminal records. As public outrage grew, the facility became a hub for protest activity.

“We are always on edge because there are always protests out here. I thought of 9/11 when I saw the fire,” a local parking lot attendant told amNewYork. “The police came fast.”

FBI agents could be seen gathering evidence throughout the day, including the alleged airsoft rifle he used during the attack.

Why are we turning over asylum seekers to Iran on a silver platter?"
text:
Even as the U.S. waged war with Iran and encouraged its citizens to take to the streets, the Trump administration was working with the regime to fast-track the deportations of dissidents, according to a new lawsuit.

Since March 2025, the U.S. government has been sharing the personal details of asylum seekers' cases with the Iranian regime, according to the suit filed earlier this month by the left-leaning Public Citizen Litigation Group and the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund (ALDF).

It alleges the U.S. government has welcomed regime officials into U.S. immigration detention centres to intimidate Iranians into returning to a country where they could face imprisonment, torture or death.

"We have a tradition of trying to be a beacon of hope for those fleeing political persecution and religious persecution, and we betrayed those confidences," Connecticut immigration attorney Cyrus Mehri, ALDF's co-founder, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal. "It just breaks my heart."

Detainees describe meetings with regime officials

The U.S. government has denied the allegations, which have not been proven in court.

But the ALDF says it has gathered multiple corroborating accounts that paint a stark picture of two seemingly enemy states working in collaboration against those fleeing persecution.

The non-profit has filed 11 sworn statements from Iranian asylum seekers in Customs and Enforcement (ICE) custody.

They include Christian converts, anti-regime protesters and 2SLGBTQ+ individuals who recounted being harassed, beaten, arrested and tortured by the Iranian regime.

One woman said in her sworn statement that she was waiting in an Arizona detention facility for her asylum claim to be processed, when she and several other Iranian detainees were taken to a room to meet with a man described by ICE agents as an Iranian consular official.

"When I saw him, I felt cold," the woman, identified only as P.M., said in her hand-written declaration. "He looked like the regime guys."

The man had a list of the Iranian detainees' names, she wrote, and knew intricate details about their asylum claims, including information they had only disclosed to U.S. immigration officials.

S.O., another asylum seeker at the at the same Arizona facility, wrote in a sworn statement that the presence of an Iranian official spread fear among the Iranian asylum seekers.

"Many of us fled Iran to escape repression, political persecution or religious harassment," S.O. wrote. "His presence inside a U.S. detention facility was terrifying."

The asylum seekers all said the Iranian officials they met with urged them to sign documents agreeing to return to Iran.

Several said they were threatened with deportation to Africa if they declined to sign.

An inside source

Mehri says those first-hand accounts are backed up by details from a senior Iranian official who reached out to him in March 2026 to warn about a new immigration policy between the U.S. and Iran.

"Under this stark policy, the U.S. was seeking the help of the Islamic regime to get rid of people from Iran fleeing Iran that are lawfully knocking on the doors of America," Mehri said.

The lawsuit does not name the official who spoke with Mehri, but says he works with the Iranian Interests Section of the Pakistani Embassy in Washington, D.C., which provides de facto consular and diplomatic services between the Iran and the U.S.

The source claimed the two governments held monthly meetings to share information about hundreds of asylum cases. These meetings, the lawsuit says, were followed by several mass deportation flights to Iran, as reported by New York Times.

"I specifically asked him, 'Did the United States government institute protocols or get assurances for the safety of Woman Life Freedom protesters, pro-democracy protesters?' " Mehri said. "The answer was no."

Nor were there any procedures in place to protect Christian or 2SLGBTQ+ Iranians, he said.

The meetings stopped before Feb. 28, when war broke out between Iran and the U.S., the lawsuit says.

But even as the conflict raged on, the lawsuit alleges ICE has "continued to mail or hand deliver document packages to the Iranian Interests Section."

"Don't forget, we're at war with Iran. Why are we turning over asylum seekers to Iran on a silver platter?" Mehri said. "It seems like the U.S. government and Iranian government can't seem to agree on anything, except for this."

Suit wants halt on sharing info with Iran

The lawsuit, filed in Federal District Court in Washington, D.C., names ICE, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as defendants.

DHS, which oversees ICE, has denied any wrongdoing.

“These allegations that ICE shared asylum application records with the Iranian government are FALSE," a DHS spokesperson told CBC in an email.

“ICE is committed to ensuring that illegal aliens are informed of their right to communicate with their consular representatives. Consistent with established protocols, ICE provides illegal aliens the opportunity to contact their consular post and facilitates consular access to detained individuals, in accordance with applicable laws, regulations, and agency policy."

The State Department did not respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit calls on the U.S. government to immediately halt information sharing with Iran, to disclose to any current asylum seekers if their privacy has been compromised and to cease the mass deportation of Iranians.

"This has to end immediately," Mehri said. "America is better than this."

Federal courts have temporarily blocked or postponed TPS terminations for, Burma (Myanmar), Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, Syria and Yemen that were scheduled to end between November 2025 and May 2026.

TPS beneficiaries from these countries retain legal status and work authorization, for now.

Employers should review affected Form I-9s and complete Supplement B reverification, where required, using the applicable court-ordered employment authorization extension date.

Burma (Myanmar)

Ethiopia

Somalia

South Sudan

Syria

Yemen

TPS beneficiaries from the above countries retain their legal status.

Burma (Myanmar) – 7/27/26

Complete Supplement B (Reverification and Rehire), if applicable;

Record the applicable employment authorization expiration date reflected in the chart;

text:
President Donald Trump's border czar Tom Homan said Monday he wants body cameras "as soon as possible" for ICE officers as the Department of Homeland Security faces escalating pressure to speed up camera rollout in the wake of two deadly shootings.

Homan, speaking to reporters outside the White House, said that body cameras were purchased for officers nationwide and as of last week ICE was "training the trainers" on how to teach officers to use the cameras.

DHS promised months ago to equip ICE agents with body cameras, but questions about the speed of the deployment surfaced this month after ICE officers who were not wearing cameras killed two people in Maine and Houston. Neither of the people killed was the intended target of the enforcement operation.

Homan has blamed the pace of the rollout on Democrats in Congress, claiming the spring government shutdown delayed necessary funding for the equipment.

He said on Monday that it took significant time and resources for ICE to hire staff, build out storage capability, and prepare for an influx of FOIA requests once the cameras were in use.

"As soon as possible, if I had it my way," he said on the timeline for full deployment.

But a cadre of Democratic senators -- along with Maine independent Sen. Angus King -- pushed back against that narrative in a Sunday letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, claiming DHS "has had more than sufficient time and funding" to distribute the cameras.

The senators noted that acting ICE director David Venturella told members of Congress the cameras would be in place by the end of July and said they saw the "timeline not as a projection, but as a firm, binding commitment." Rep. Sylvia Garcia said recently that Venturella made the same promise to her.

The practice of vehicle stops -- the operation that led to both deadly shootings this month -- has in particular drawn scrutiny. The Department suspended most vehicle stops early last week but Trump overturned the decision less than 24 hours later.

Homan confirmed on Monday that that all vehicle stops must involve at least one person with a working body camera and that officers would be required to have their cameras on for the duration of the stop.

Homan maintained there were no other policy changes planned for officers and pushed off questions about the vetting of the ICE officer who shot Johan Sebastian Guerrero in Maine last week.

"That's a question for ICE. That's under investigation. I'm sure that part now is part of the investigation," Homan said in reference to the officer's alleged history. "We'll let the investigation play out."

"I can't speak for everyone in the administration, but quality agents are very important," Homan added. "If you're going to give somebody a badge and gun, they need to be the best they can be."

Homan also denied a report from The New York Times that the FBI would no longer be involved in investigating assaults on ICE officers. The FBI and DHS wrote in a statement that the reporting was "false" and that the "FBI will continue to investigate in accordance with agency policy."

"The FBI is still going to continue to lead shooting investigations. As far as I'm concerned, I'm not aware of any change in policy, and I think the FBI and DHS actually pushed back on that story," Homan said Monday.

text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Delia C. Ramirez (IL-03) joined Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), with the support of House Democratic Leadership, to officially announce and sign a discharge petition to force a vote on the bipartisan American Dream and Promise Act.

The American Dream and Promise Act would provide eligible Dreamers, undocumented individuals who were brought into the U.S. as children, with an earned pathway to citizenship and allow eligible recipients of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) and Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) to obtain lawful permanent resident status.

A discharge petition allows a majority of House members - 218 members - to force the House to vote on the American Dream and Promise Act.

“This is not a warning about what might happen. Dreamers are losing their jobs, being detained, and being deported right now. Temporary Protected Status holders who have lived here for decades are being told to prepare to leave. Congress has the power to stop this, and there is no excuse for hiding behind Speaker Johnson while families are torn apart,” said Congresswoman Garcia. “The overwhelming majority of Americans support a path to citizenship for Dreamers. So I am calling on my colleagues from both sides of the aisle to listen to their constituents. Sign the petition. Force the vote. Put these protections into law.”

“For decades, Dreamers and TPS holders, many here since the age of two, have been waiting for stability. They have grown up here, taken care of us and given so much to our communities, yet they're living in constant fear of being ripped away from the only home they know. The growing attacks of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court on Dreamers and immigrants make it clear how urgent it is for Congress to finally act. That is why I am proud to join Congresswoman Garcia and advocates in filing a discharge petition to bring the Dream and Promise Act for a vote," said Congresswoman Ramirez. "Democrats and Republicans alike need to prove to every Dreamer and immigrant that we know they are part of the fabric of our nation and finally create their pathway for citizenship. Let's pass the Dream and Promise Act."

“Dreamers and TPS holders are our neighbors, essential workers, and community leaders. They help power key industries including construction, health care, agriculture, and child care. They are the parents of hundreds of thousands of U.S. citizen children, working to provide for their families and integral members of communities across the country,” said Todd Schulte, President of FWD.us. “The Supreme Court’s decision allowing the termination of TPS along with the administration's quiet, ongoing attacks on Dreamers – with and without DACA – means all of them are now at greater risk of deportation. We’re grateful for Congresswoman Garcia’s leadership on the Discharge Petition for the Dream and Promise Act to ensure Dreamers and TPS holders are able to keep living, working, and contributing to our country. Every Member who says they support Dreamers and TPS holders should sign the Discharge Petition.”

Background:

Under the Trump Administration, immigrant communities, including DACA recipients and TPS holders, have been under attack. In April, 2026, the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) made a decision that makes Dreamers even more vulnerable by allowing ICE to begin removal proceedings, effectively rendering their DACA protections obsolete. As of January 2026, there were over 260 documented arrests of DACA recipients, and 174 recipients were deported. June 2025, the Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration had the authority to end TPS status without congressional consent, putting more than 350,000 TPS holders at risk of deportation and countless more asylum seekers’ lives in danger.

text:
In our recent post, Reading the Fine Print: USCIS Clarifies TPS Placeholder Dates Following Supreme Court Ruling, we discussed US Citizenship and Immigration Services’ (USCIS) use of temporary “placeholder” expiration dates for certain Temporary Protected Status (TPS) beneficiaries following the Supreme Court’s May 2026 decision and related litigation.

Notably, Haiti remains listed with a July 24, 2026 placeholder date. Because that date has not yet arrived, we do not currently expect a further Haiti-specific update today. However, given the pace of recent developments, employers should continue to monitor USCIS announcements closely.

As we noted in our prior post, these placeholder dates do not represent final decisions regarding TPS validity or employment authorization. Rather, they are temporary dates tied to ongoing litigation and agency implementation efforts and may be revised again with little notice.

Employers Should Also Take Note of Recent M-274 Updates

While much attention has focused on the rapidly changing TPS placeholder dates, employers should also review USCIS’s recent update to the M-274 Handbook for Employers (Sections 5.0 through 5.3), which reflects the employment authorization changes implemented under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA). These changes have been detailed in prior BLOG posts on August 15, 2025 and October 30, 2025. USCIS noted that “In most cases, these developments have reduced or eliminated the automatic extension periods for qualifying TPS applicants and beneficiaries with TPS-based EADs.” Additionally, the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) interim final rule, effective Oct. 30, 2025, and USCIS’ implementation of H.R. 1 on July 22, 2025, also affected other EAD categories.

The revised guidance addresses automatic EAD extension rules, TPS-related work authorization, and reverification obligations that may affect employers independent of the ongoing TPS litigation. As a result, employers should review both the updated TPS placeholder dates, the USCIS TPS page and the revised M-274 guidance when assessing upcoming Form I-9 reverification requirements for affected employees. In some cases, the dates reflected in both USCIS’ TPS guidance and the automatic extension rules applicable to a particular EAD renewal application will need to be analyzed to determine an employee’s continuing work authorization.

As a refresher, the OBBA significantly changed the rules governing TPS-based EADs. Under the OBBA, TPS-based EADs are generally limited to a one-year validity period, with the possibility of a one-year extension if certain requirements are met. Individuals who had a TPS-based EAD renewal application pending as of July 22, 2025, may be eligible for an automatic extension of employment authorization for up to 540 days, but not beyond July 22, 2026. For certain TPS beneficiaries who filed EAD renewal applications between July 22, 2025, and October 30, 2025, the automatic extension period may instead be limited to one year from the EAD’s “Card Expires” date and remains subject to the July 22, 2026 statutory limitation implemented by the OBBA.

With several TPS-related employment authorization deadlines approaching and litigation continuing in Massachusetts challenging portions of USCIS’s implementation of OBBA, employers should expect additional developments in the coming weeks. The Seyfarth team will continue monitoring both the litigation and USCIS guidance and will provide updates as new information becomes available.

title: Fact-check: Trump administration says 250000 noncitizens are registered to vote in 4 states
authors: Amy Sherman and Louis Jacobson, PolitiFact reporters, Amy Sherman, Louis Jacobson, PolitiFact reporters
description:
As the 2026 midterms approach, the Trump administration is seeking voting data from states, though many leaders have refused.
“We’ve identified 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in just four states,” he said.
Second, the DHS data does not answer whether registered noncitizens ever cast a ballot — much less had a decisive impact on any election results.
Neither Mullin nor his department said how many of the 250,000 noncitizens voted and over what period.
In 2024, Ohio Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose referred 597 apparent noncitizen registered voters for prosecution.
text:
In back-to-back events, President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin spotlighted noncitizen voting as a threat to the U.S. election system — even though years of evidence shows it is a statistical rarity with no impact on election results.

Trump’s July 16 primetime address continued to push lawmakers to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require Americans to provide a government-issued photo ID to vote and documentary proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate, when they register. The legislation is stalled in the Senate over voter disenfranchisement concerns.

As the 2026 midterms approach, the Trump administration is seeking voting data from states, though many leaders have refused. Judges have blocked administration efforts to obtain this voter data.

In a release of documents alongside Trump’s address, the Department of Homeland Security said “over 250,000 non-citizens are illegally registered to vote in just the four states,” citing California, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada, which are all led by Democratic governors.

Mullin repeated the 250,000 figure in a July 17 news conference. “We’ve identified 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in just four states,” he said.

Is that number legitimate? Mullin presented it as a certainty, but voting experts urged caution.

First, databases are subject to errors, mistaken identities and outdated citizenship information; historically, states have found that the actual number of noncitizens registered to vote drops significantly once a large-sounding number is vetted for accuracy.

Second, the DHS data does not answer whether registered noncitizens ever cast a ballot — much less had a decisive impact on any election results. Trump and Mullin’s rhetoric gives the unsupported impression that they did.

While Trump has spotlighted allegations of noncitizen voters for more than a decade, it is illegal for noncitizens to cast a ballot in federal races. Violations are “routinely investigated and prosecuted,” but there is “no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome,” the Bipartisan Policy Center concluded in February.

Let’s take a closer look at what the buzzy 250,000 figure could mean — and what it doesn’t.

How did DHS calculate this number?

Homeland Security broke down its count of “potential” noncitizen registered voters by state, using more cautious language than Mullin:

California: 190,832

New Jersey: 35,152

Nevada: 15,903

Pennsylvania: 14,576

Each state’s number represents less than 1% of the state’s registered voters.

Neither Mullin’s remarks nor a department press release explain how the 250,000 figure was collected. A response to PolitiFact’s inquiry did not provide any additional details.

David Becker, an elections expert who attended a White House briefing this week, cited a White House official saying the data comparisons were done with commercial data. Becker said that data does not allow a comparison to public voter files because it lacks personally identifiable information such as driver’s license or Social Security numbers.

“You’re going to create a lot of false matches because of that,” Becker told reporters in a July 17 webinar.

This year, with encouragement from the Trump administration, several states have used SAVE — short for Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements — to make initial estimates of the number of noncitizen voters on their rolls. SAVE is a federal web service that government agencies can use to verify the immigration status of applicants seeking benefits such as Medicaid, housing loans and unemployment compensation.

It’s not clear what data and methodology federal immigration officials used for the review of the four Democratic-run states. Homeland Security said those states had not used the SAVE system.

Officials from the targeted states treated the 250,000 figure with skepticism.

Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar said the “numbers are wildly speculative at best and the Department of Homeland Security hasn’t shared anything that backs it up.”

Pennsylvania Secretary of State Al Schmidt said that “all evidence has shown that noncitizen voting is extremely rare across the country” and that the state will review any information by Homeland Security to evaluate the claims’ validity.

How reliable is the 250,000 figure?

Experts cited several reasons to be cautious about the headline number and how Trump and Mullin framed it.

For starters, Homeland Security’s letters to state officials used more cautious language — glossed over in public remarks by Trump and Mullin — that called it a “preliminary review” and said that there “may be as many as” the number of noncitizens they found on the voter rolls.

At his press conference, Mullin did not identify the individuals as potential noncitizens; he simply called them “noncitizens.”

Another reason for caution is history.

In the past, when government officials have announced initial numbers of noncitizens on voter rolls, those figures have dropped dramatically after months of vetting by state and local officials and the media.

In 2012, then-Florida Gov. Rick Scott ordered state officials to clear the rolls of noncitizen voters ahead of the election.

Florida initially assembled a list of about 180,000 potential noncitizens. With more scrutiny, however, officials whittled the count to about 2,600 names, then 198, then 85. The initial list was rife with errors, even flagging a Brooklyn-born World War II veteran.

Texas officials have also found errors when looking for noncitizen voters. In April, then-Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson wrote a letter to federal immigration officials raising concerns about the data’s accuracy, Votebeat reported. The state has flagged about 2,000 potential noncitizens on the voter rolls.

“As my staff has informed you, county voter registrars have obtained citizenship documentation from some Texas voters who were identified in the SAVE system as potential non-citizens,” Nelson wrote. “We are aware of instances in which state driver’s license records inaccurately reflect a person’s current citizenship status.”

Nelson added that some people had been mistakenly registered to vote because of clerical errors by a voter registrar, even after the person had acknowledged on a voter registration application that they were not U.S. citizens.

Did they vote?

A natural question when discussing election integrity: Did illegal voting occur?

Neither Mullin nor his department said how many of the 250,000 noncitizens voted and over what period.

State reviews in recent years have found that few noncitizens actually cast ballots even if they’re registered.

Georgia officials said they have found about 139 votes cast by noncitizens out of 32 million votes cast since 1992.

In 2024, Ohio Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose referred 597 apparent noncitizen registered voters for prosecution. Of that number, he said 138 cast ballots.

text:
Following killings in Maine and Texas, Oregon senators join colleagues calling for reforms, body-worn camera deployment, and independent investigations

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley today demanded stronger accountability measures for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers., urging the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to fulfill its previous commitments to deploy and expand the usage of body-worn cameras, strengthen officer identification requirements, and review enforcement protocols.

The measures suggested by the Oregon senators along with more than 30 of their colleagues in a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin seek to help prevent future deadly encounters involving ICE enforcement officers – and comes after two recent fatal shootings during immigration enforcement operations in Biddeford, Maine, and Houston, Texas.

“The recent fatal shootings involving U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers, specifically within U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), in Biddeford, Maine, and Houston, Texas, coupled with similar incidents elsewhere in the country, are completely unacceptable,” the senators wrote. “Rather than making our communities safer, these actions endanger our citizens and seriously undermine confidence in law enforcement generally.”

“The tragic deaths of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Joan Sebastian Durán Guerrero occurred less than a week apart and carry startling similarities,” the senators continued. “In both incidents, the individuals were killed in enforcement actions in which they were not the intended targets. Furthermore, both individuals were shot by DHS officials while inside a vehicle. The unnecessary loss of life in these incidents demands immediate, thorough, independent, and transparent investigations (including the full involvement of local and state law enforcement personnel) along with a comprehensive examination of enforcement protocols, training, and operational approaches necessary to prevent such tragedies. These recent events have further compromised the credibility of DHS and fractured public trust within communities across our country. In each case, DHS quickly issued statements asserting that officers were acting in self-defense, even before evidence of the facts surrounding the incidents had been gathered. Compounding this failure, no DHS officials involved in these fatal shootings wore body-worn cameras that could be reviewed by investigators or members of the public.”

“We remain supportive of removing dangerous convicted criminals from our communities, but this goal can and must be achieved without endangering these very communities in the process,” the senators finished. “The American people deserve clarity and accountability. We urge you to honor your Department’s earlier commitments and take immediate action to implement these necessary reforms. We also stand ready to work with you to codify reforms into law.”

In addition to Wyden and Merkley, other co-signers of the letter led by U.S. Senator Angus King (I-ME) are U.S. Senators Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Patty Murray (D-WA), Dick Durbin (D-IL), Gary Peters (D-MI), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), Chris Coons (D-DE), Jack Reed (D-RI), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Maggie Hassan (D-NH), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Peter Welch (D-VT), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Tina Smith (D-MN), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), John Hickenlooper (D-CO), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Mark Warner (D-VA), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), and John Fetterman (D-PA).

title: New court filing raises questions about DHS plans for Roxbury ICE detention center
description:

text:
The latest filing contradicts a court notice from last week that said the agency intended to move forward with the Morris County project.

A new federal court filing shows that the Department of Homeland Security has not decided whether to convert a massive Morris County warehouse into an immigrant detention center, despite filing court papers just a week ago saying the agency intended to move forward with the project.

In a joint status report filed Friday in the U.S. District Court, Justice Department attorneys said DHS is “continuing to assess whether to proceed with plans to convert the Roxbury warehouse into a detention facility,” but said there is no timeline for a decision.

The latest filing appears to contradict a court notice the Trump administration filed just a week earlier stating that DHS “intends to move forward with plans to consider the retrofitting” of the 470,000-square-foot warehouse on Route 46.

That filing had itself reversed the administration’s position from nine days earlier, when Justice Department attorneys told the court DHS no longer planned to convert the warehouse into a detention center and instead intended to sell the property.

None of the court filings explain the agency’s reversals.

Asked about the latest filing, a DHS spokesperson referred The Jersey Vindicator to a month-old social media post from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who said the agency would “NEVER back down” despite Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s statement that DHS had abandoned the project.

The agency ignored The Vindicator’s attempts to further clarify its plans. As The Vindicator first reported, DHS purchased the warehouse in February for $129.3 million from DG Roxbury Property Owner LP, a Delaware limited partnership tied to Dallas-based Dalfen Industrial and a Goldman Sachs asset management fund.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement initially sought to convert the sprawling building into a processing center for newly detained immigrants swept up in President Donald Trump’s mass deportation raids.

The Roxbury warehouse is one of 11 industrial properties DHS purchased nationwide for about $1 billion that would dramatically increase the agency’s detention capacity. Federal planning documents show the Roxbury facility alone could hold as many as 1,500 people.

Federal officials later disputed that number in court, claiming the facility would hold fewer than 550 detainees. Recent national reporting has suggested that the administration has retreated from the strategy because of lawsuits, community opposition, and significant infrastructure problems.

Still, activists in Roxbury organized major protests and packed local government meetings, which in turn pushed officials in the Republican-dominated town to join a state lawsuit against DHS and ICE seeking to stop the project.

That suit, filed in March, accused federal officials of ignoring laws that require environmental reviews and consultations with state and local governments.

According to court filings, DHS ignored Roxbury officials for two months and did not respond until after the department bought the warehouse.

“And when DHS did respond, it did not ask for input on environmental or other local impacts, but simply confirmed its plans to plow ahead with the detention facility,” attorneys for the state and township wrote.

Environmental groups have warned that the detention camp could increase pollution, snarl traffic, and threaten environmentally sensitive land in a protected region that supplies drinking water to millions in the Garden State.

In May, ICE agreed to halt most work at the site while it conducted an environmental assessment. Under the consent order, ICE can install fencing, security cameras, and alarms, and perform basic property maintenance, but broader conversion work remains on hold.

The constant whiplash over the project’s future drew a blistering response from David Broderick, a board member of NJ Appleseed and legal counsel for Project No ICE North Jersey Alliance, or Project NINJA, a volunteer coalition of community, religious, environmental, civil rights, and activist groups fighting ICE detention facilities in North Jersey.

“Given the impracticality of converting the warehouse into a detention facility, which presumably led to DHS’s original decision, one can’t help but suspect that this is nothing more than a political charade designed to embarrass state and local leaders, who declared victory at the time of the DOJ’s original filing,” Broderick said after the feds said they were resurrecting plans for the site.

“The DHS reversal is yet another example of the chaos that seems to engulf the Trump administration at every turn,” he continued. “In any event, DHS can be sure that this action has even further enraged and motivated their opponents.”

title: ICE's latest arrest of a Houston ISD student prompts pushback from his supporters
description:
A rising senior in Houston ISD who was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents Friday was released from detention on Monday, according to U.S. Rep. Lizzie Fletcher, D-Houston.
An ICE spokesperson over the weekend confirmed the arrest of Alim Garipov, an 18-year-old student from Russia who attends Bellaire High School.
"We are relieved and grateful that Alim has finally been released from detention and reunited with his family,” the statement also said.
"I cannot say enough good things about Alim," the Bellaire employee said.
Editor’s note: This story was updated July 20, 2026, after U.S. Rep. Lizzie Fletcher released a statement saying Alim Garipov had been released from ICE detention.
text:
A rising senior in Houston ISD who was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents Friday was released from detention on Monday, according to U.S. Rep. Lizzie Fletcher, D-Houston.

An ICE spokesperson over the weekend confirmed the arrest of Alim Garipov, an 18-year-old student from Russia who attends Bellaire High School. The agency said Garipov was allowed entry into the U.S. in May 2022, but was permitted to stay in the country for only six months.

Fletcher, in what her office described as a joint statement Monday night with Garipov’s family and an immigration attorney, said the teen was released after a “community-wide advocacy effort.”

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

"We are relieved and grateful that Alim has finally been released from detention and reunited with his family,” the statement also said. “This outcome came after a tireless, expeditious effort over the weekend, working in partnership to secure Alim's release.”

ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment and confirmation Monday night.

Friends of the Garipov family previously told Houston Public Media they were in the process of making an asylum claim to stay in the country legally.

"A pending application does not confer any type of legal status in the United States," an ICE spokesperson said in a weekend statement after Garipov’s arrest. "If a person enters our country illegally, they are subject to detention or deportation."

Garipov is not the first Houston ISD student to be detained by ICE during the second term of President Donald Trump, whose administration has ramped up immigration-related arrests and deportations.

Trends under Trump

Earlier this year, Mauro Henriquez, a senior at Sam Houston Math, Science, and Technology Center, was deported to Honduras after spending months in the Montgomery Processing Center. Henriquez was detained Dec. 16 alongside his father during a scheduled appointment with ICE agents. Initially the two were detained together. Henriquez was later separated from his father and moved to a detention facility in Livingston on Feb. 12.

Henriquez's prolonged detention sparked outrage in the community as more than 100 of his classmates protested outside of their high school in early February, demanding his release and changes to ICE operations throughout the city and country.

RELATED: Texas state leaders target school walkouts as students rally for Houston teen detained by ICE

Nationally, arrests and deportations have surged during Trump's second term, during which several people in Texas and across the country have died during interactions with ICE agents. Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old father of three, was shot and killed by an ICE agent on July 7 in Houston's East End.

The Houston Chronicle reported in February the immigrant population in Houston ISD dropped by nearly 4,000 students – or roughly half of the total enrollment drop this year. In a presentation to the Houston City Council in September, state-appointed superintendent Mike Miles suggested enrollment declines may be due to heightened ICE activity under the Trump administration.

"Too many immigrant families in our community and across the country are facing similar uncertainty and separation, and we are actively working to help many others facing the same fear,” said the joint statement released by Fletcher’s office Monday night. "We will continue working to help members of our community in these challenging times, and we will continue to advocate for an end to the unfair and unjust policies that led to this heartbreaking situation in the first place.”

"Best person I know"

Garipov is from a rural village in western Russia, according to a Bellaire employee who asked to remain anonymous for fear of losing their job. The employee said Garipov was captain of the school's swim team last year and has a 3.97 unweighted GPA.

"I cannot say enough good things about Alim," the Bellaire employee said.

The employee said Garipov's aunt reached out to them late Friday night, hours after he was detained at Hobby Airport. The aunt asked for Bellaire teachers to send character reference letters to help with Garipov's case, the employee said.

"I sent her a letter at about 1:30 a.m. vouching for him, his character, his contribution to Bellaire High School, how amazing this young man is, how fortunate we are as a country to have his contributions," the school employee said.

RELATED: Houston ISD soccer standout deported to Honduras after months in ICE detention

A review of Garipov's resume, which was provided to Houston Public Media by the Bellaire employee, shows he has worked as a tutor and swim coach and was spending his summer as an assistant to graduate students in the biodesign lab at Rice University.

In short essays compiled for a college admissions recommendation letter, Garipov detailed his life as an immigrant since coming to the United States as a 14-year-old without knowing how to speak English. He wrote about working hard to learn the language and shouldering many household responsibilities as the strongest English-speaker in his home. Garipov wrote about navigating taxes, bills, medical appointments, asylum paperwork and insurance for his parents.

"I started from zero and didn’t let that stop me," Garipov wrote. "Every time the work got harder – whether it was new vocabulary, new subjects, or a new culture – I pushed through instead of pulling back."

Shepherd Gibson is a classmate and close friend to Garipov.

"He is the best person I know. He tries his best at everything," Gibson said before breaking down over Garipov’s detention.

Editor’s note: This story was updated July 20, 2026, after U.S. Rep. Lizzie Fletcher released a statement saying Alim Garipov had been released from ICE detention.

description:
A Trump-appointed federal judge on Monday tossed out a Department of Justice lawsuit that aimed to invalidate state and local “sanctuary” policies, which limit information-sharing and cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and immigration enforcement.
It preceded Operation Metro Surge, during which thousands of immigration agents arrested thousands of immigrants; shot three people, killing two; and sparked major protests.

text:
A Trump-appointed federal judge on Monday tossed out a Department of Justice lawsuit that aimed to invalidate state and local “sanctuary” policies, which limit information-sharing and cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and immigration enforcement.

The lawsuit, filed in September, was one of at least 27 such cases filed against more than 20 cities, counties and states during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term. It preceded Operation Metro Surge, during which thousands of immigration agents arrested thousands of immigrants; shot three people, killing two; and sparked major protests.

Leaders at the Department of Homeland Security repeatedly pointed to state and local governments’ refusal to assist in immigration enforcement as a reason for not ending the operation sooner.

In its complaint, the DOJ challenged several state and local policies: a Minnesota law preventing the state Department of Driver and Vehicle Services from sharing data with immigration agencies; Minneapolis and St. Paul policies barring local police from enforcing immigration laws; an attorney general’s legal advisory prohibiting Minnesota law enforcement agencies from holding someone based on a request from federal immigration authorities if the person would otherwise be released from custody; and a Hennepin County policy modeled on that attorney general’s advisory.

Eric C. Tostrud, chief judge for the District of Minnesota, dismissed all of the claims. He primarily cited the Tenth Amendment’s anticommandeering doctrine, which prohibits the federal government from forcing state and local authorities to carry out tasks — such as immigration enforcement — which are the sole responsibility of the federal government.

text:
A federal judge has ordered immigration officials to release a 32-year-old Florida resident from custody after she spent the last ten days in the U.S. Immigration of Customs Enforcement field office near the Burlington Mall.

Maria Rosales was arrested on July 10 at Logan Airport after coming to town for a Noah Kahan concert, and held in the controversial facility while her lawyers argued for her release.

In a sworn affidavit obtained by WBUR, Rosales detailed "tough" and "uncomfortable" conditions similar to those reported over the last year by other Burlington detainees, and which have drawn scrutiny from members of Congress and the public.

"We have to beg for water ... We've been in the same clothes for weeks ... The room is extremely hot with all those bodies in a tiny cell ... The food is inedible," she wrote in the affidavit. "Some of the girls here refuse to eat because the food is vile and they couldn't stomach it."

Rosales said she didn't always have access to a shower, and that her request for Tylenol while she was on her period was "disregarded."

She also wrote that she and other detainees "have to beg for phone time to speak to our lawyers and family," and that one day, "the officers got angry and claimed the phones were down all day."

Rosales was born in Colombia and came to the U.S. with her parents when she was 4-years-old, her lawyer Todd Pomerleau said in an interview. She grew up in Florida, he said, and leads a performing arts nonprofit for youth. Her affidavit said she is studying at Miami Dade College to be a nurse.

She has had legal status in the U.S. under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, or DACA, which was established under former President Barack Obama to give temporary status and work authorization to undocumented immigrants brought to the country as children.

According to Pomerleau, Rosales applied to renew her DACA status three years ago and her case is pending. So she was surprised when ICE agents stopped her at Logan. They told her she had a deportation order from 2017 — the same year she’d originally applied for DACA — and had allegedly missed a court date. According to her affidavit, she was not presented with an arrest warrant at Logan.

Pomerleau suspects the ordeal stems from an incident in 2017 when Rosales and her family were briefly stopped at a border checkpoint while driving across the country.

"I believe I am a worthy member of society," she wrote in her affidavit. "I was unaware I had an order of deportation in 2017. If I knew I had a court date, I would have attended."

As WBUR has previously reported, the field office was not designed to be a long-term holding center; it's an intake center, where immigrants arrested by ICE are brought for booking before being moved to longer-term detention centers.

But beginning sometime in the spring of 2025, as the Trump administration launched a major immigration effort in Massachusetts, many arrested by ICE found themselves stuck in the building's small concrete holding cells for days — and sometimes weeks.

Some, like Milford high school student Marcelo Gomes da Silva, have said they were held with dozens of other people in a single room. Others said they weren't given access to showers or sanitary supplies. And many described sleeping on concrete floors with just a mylar blanket.

"These claims that there are subprime conditions or overcrowding are false," a spokesperson for ICE said in an email. "The ICE Burlington facility has an abundance of supplies, including food, assorted snacks, water, personal hygiene, and bedding materials."

A federal court ruling in June said ICE would have to seek permission to hold people for more than 12 hours at an administrative office like the one in Burlington. The ICE spokesperson did not say if the agency had obtained that permission here.

Pomerleau said he’s heard similar complaints about the conditions in Burlington from several other clients over the last year, including some of the women arrested at an Allston carwash last November.

"They were held there, six to 10 days," he said. "One of them they were feeding donuts to was a diabetic,” and her blood sugar had spiked by the time she was released.

The day after Rosales was arrested and brought to the Burlington ICE office, her lawyer filed what's known as a habeas petition in federal court to challenge her detention and prevent the government from transferring her out of Massachusetts. A judge granted the petition the same day.

The federal government filed its response July 16, claiming Rosales was still eligible for deportation, Pomerleau said.

"They claim pending DACA renewal doesn’t prevent deportation," he said. "We strongly disagreee."

On Monday, the judge seemed to agree. He ordered ICE to release Rosales by 7 p.m. and said she could not be re-arrested "absent compliance with the applicable statutory and regulatory procedures."

Pomerleau said his colleagues attempted to visit Rosales in Burlington this past Friday, but were initially denied entrance. They were eventually allowed in to speak with her, though immigration officials brought them all to a private conference room, so they did not see the space where she was being held.

"She said it's the worst treatment she's had in her life. She's begging for water, sanitary supplies," Pomerleau said. "It just seems like there's all these health code violations."

Since last year, when accounts of conditions at the Burlington facility first began to surface, local officials have sought access for building department staff to inspect it for zoning or health violations. A judge denied the town's request for a court order last fall, in part because she said the detainee accounts presented as evidence in the case were too old.

Rosales' case could present a new opening for town officials.

"We are aware of what has happened to Ms. Rosales and it’s as distressing as all of the stories and accounts we have heard coming from 1000 District Ave.," said Burlington select board member Mike Espejo. "Our goal to get our building inspector in there has not changed and we will continue to try and accomplish that through all available legal channels."

title: Attacks on human dignity can never be normalized, say 2 US bishops after deadly ICE shootings
description:
Two U.S. Catholic bishops are lamenting recent deadly immigration enforcement encounters, calling for God-given human dignity to be respected in every individual.
On July 14, ICE agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian, after being stopped by ICE agents near a laundromat.
The Trump administration briefly halted, then resumed, ICE traffic stops in the wake of the deaths.
"Our pastoral concerns are distinct from what the civil law itself may permit," said the two bishops.
In a report released in June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights counted 52 deaths in ICE custody during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration.
text:
Two U.S. Catholic bishops are lamenting recent deadly immigration enforcement encounters, calling for God-given human dignity to be respected in every individual.

"As Catholics, we believe that all persons are created in the image and likeness of God and, therefore, grieve all situations where human life is brought to an unnatural end. This is a core teaching of our faith and one we can never grow weary of proclaiming as disciples of Our Lord Jesus Christ," said Bishop Daniel E. Garcia of Austin, Texas, and Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Victoria, Texas.

The two issued a July 20 joint pastoral reflection as chairs, respectively, of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Subcommittee for the Promotion of Racial Justice and Reconciliation and the USCCB's Committee on Migration.

Their statement follows three separate deaths recorded days apart in July amid operations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers as they implement the Trump administration's hardline crackdown on immigration.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Houston area man, was fatally shot en route to work in his vehicle July 7 during an ICE traffic stop. On July 14, ICE agents shot and killed 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian, after being stopped by ICE agents near a laundromat. Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, a 28-year-old man from Mexico, was struck and killed by a tractor trailer July 15 in St. Augustine, Florida, while fleeing ICE and Homeland Security agents on foot.

ICE's claims that Salgado and Durán attempted to ram officials with their respective vehicles have been disputed, with Houston law enforcement officials expressing frustration over the federal agency's lack of collaboration in investigating forensic evidence in Salgado's death.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that Salgado — a Mexican national who had been in the U.S. for some 35 years, and who was in the process of obtaining legal authorization to reside and work in the country — was not the intended target of the ICE operation in which he died.

In Colorado, an employee of the GEO Group — a private firm that contracts with ICE to operate its Aurora processing center — opened fire July 16 on a protester at the site, injuring the woman's foot.

The Trump administration briefly halted, then resumed, ICE traffic stops in the wake of the deaths.

In their statement, Bishops Garcia and Cahill quoted from the USCCB's November 2025 special pastoral message on immigration: "We are disturbed when we see among our people a climate of fear and anxiety around questions of profiling and immigration enforcement."

Drawing on the USCCB's 2018 pastoral letter on racism, "Open Wide Our Hearts," the bishops stressed that "racial profiling in particular violates God-given dignity," adding the practice "also inflicts profound harm on individuals, families, and communities by fostering fear, eroding trust, and increasing the risk of unjust and even tragic outcomes. "

"Our pastoral concerns are distinct from what the civil law itself may permit," said the two bishops.

They warned that "acts that diminish or disregard the dignity of any person or group of people should never be normalized in our society," pointing to both "the dehumanization of immigrants, regardless of their legal status" and "the vilification of law enforcement officers" as examples.

Bishops Garcia and Cahill said they "continue to affirm the legitimate role of civil authorities to implement the law in a humane manner and with respect for fundamental human rights, including the rights to life and due process."

Underscoring that "the power of the state must always be exercised within the limits of the moral law," they called for "accountability, transparency, and justice, which require that meaningful reforms be made to our immigration system."

The bishops said they "join in praying for the souls of those killed and for their families, for our nation, and for all those entrusted with the duties of public service."

They also prayed "for an end to dehumanizing rhetoric, racial prejudice, and violence and for a renewed commitment to recognizing the inherent dignity of every person as a child of God," and pleaded for "the intercession of Mary, Our Mother, who is the model of perfect faith in times of grief, hardship, and uncertainty."

According to data analyzed by The Guardian, eight persons — including U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti — have been shot to death by federal immigration agents under the current Trump administration as of July 15, with 13 injured and another 9 other shooting incidents with no injuries.

In a report released in June, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights counted 52 deaths in ICE custody during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration. The two organizations said ICE "fails to disclose adequate information about the circumstances surrounding deaths in its custody," with medical neglect suspected as a key factor.

As of April, more than 60,000 are in ICE custody, the majority of whom (just under 71%) have no criminal convictions, according to Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

text:
With this complaint Khalil sought $20 million – or an official apology and an end to unconstitutional policy

July 20, 2026, New York – Mahmoud Khalil filed his second federal lawsuit in a week today. The latest case, against the Trump administration, seeks accountability for his wrongful arrest, wrongful detention, and other abuses. It comes on the heels of a separate lawsuit in which he sued individual members of the administration, including Stephen Miller and Marco Rubio, and three anti-Palestinian organizations – Canary Mission, Betar, and the Heritage Foundation – for conspiring to deprive him of his constitutional rights. Both filed by the Center for Constitutional Rights, the suits reflect Mr. Khalil’s resolve to push back against his persecutors 16 months into an ordeal that began when federal agents abducted him in March 2025 in retaliation for his advocacy for Palestinian rights and detained him for 104 days, forcing him to miss the birth of his first child.

For this type of lawsuit, Mr. Khalil was first required to file an administrative claim with the government; after the agencies denied the complaint and failed to address the harms it raised, he was then able to file a federal lawsuit, which he did today. His original claim was filed on July 10, 2025, and asked for $20 million in damages that he would use to help others similarly targeted by the Trump administration and Columbia University; in the claim, he said he would accept, in lieu of payment, an official apology and abandonment of the administration’s unconstitutional policy.

“Not only is the U.S. government using taxpayer dollars to fund Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, but they are weaponizing the immigration and legal systems to target those who speak out against them,” said Mr. Khalil. “There has to be accountability for political retaliation and abuse of power. With these lawsuits, I am pursuing justice against everyone who contributed to my unlawful detention and spread lies in an attempt to destroy my reputation. I’m holding the U.S. government accountable not just for myself, but for everyone they try to silence through intimidation, detention, or deportation.”

Malice marked the treatment of Mr. Khalil from the outset, as the administration sought to terrorize him and his family. Today’s suit cites a range of abuses, including false arrest, false imprisonment, abuse of the legal system, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. Mr. Khalil brings the case under the Federal Tort Claims Act, a 1946 statute that allows individuals to sue the U.S. government for civil law violations. He is seeking damages directly from the United States for torts, or wrongs, committed by officers of the State Department, the Department of Homeland Security, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. His conspiracy case, filed last Tuesday and brought under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, differs in that it names as defendants administration officials in their individual capacities and the private actors they conspired with.

“Mr. Khalil will never get back the months stolen from him when he was abducted and unlawfully held in immigration detention, leading him to miss his child’s birth and first months of life,” said Samah Sisay, a staff attorney at the Center for Constitutional Rights. “The Trump administration must take responsibility for its unconstitutional targeting of Mr. Khalil and compensate him for the severe harms that he continues to navigate due to its unlawful actions.”

Mr. Khalil was the first victim in a series of wrongful arrests of Palestinian rights advocates – a campaign by the administration to weaken the Palestinian solidarity movement and punish those who spoke out against Israel’s U.S.-enabled genocide in Gaza.

Mr. Khalil’s immigration and habeas cases are ongoing.

… Following his arrest, he was detained at the Plymouth County Correctional Facility (‘PCCF’) in Massachusetts, where he remained for a week.
